subjects.label: Jacobins under the Directory: repeated revival, containment and repression
subjects.meaning: Jacobin press, clubs and parliamentary activity revived in distinct Directorial cycles: post-Vendémiaire indulgence aided the Pantheon Club before closure; post-Fructidor constitutional circles rallied mixed anti-royalist republicans before democratic demands prompted restriction. In1799 press freedom, the Manège, appointments and emergency conscription, forced-loan and hostage measures renewed influence without a parliamentary majority. Official encouragement again gave way to hostile campaigning, eviction and Fouché’s closure of the Manège; rejection of Country in Danger contained emergency politics and served Sieyes’s constitutional-executive project. Jacobin efforts to impeach the former Directors and General Schérer rested on accusations of corruption; the indictments were ultimately rejected, not established as judicial findings.
subjects.stance: Pantheon, constitutional circles and Manège were distinct formations. Wartime emergency and anti-royalism created opportunities, but neither official encouragement nor electoral gains meant stable Jacobin control.

evidence.evidence_summary: Amnesty, press subsidies, renewed meetings, and the thousand-member Pantheon Club mark rapid Jacobin recovery.

Initial division over Babeuf gave way to sympathy after his wife’s arrest and applause for reunion with the Jacobins. The government then closed clubs and a theatre, purged suspects and criminalized advocacy of the1793constitution; sympathy is not proof of conspiracy membership.
Post-Fructidor clubs and constitutional circles formed across departments as intended republican rallying points, drawing many veterans of the revolutionary left.
Social and democratic demands and calls to widen suffrage led to closures; circles nevertheless helped defeat official candidates in the elections.
Press freedom, the Manège Club, official appointments, conscription, and a forced loan mark renewed Jacobin influence.

Hostage law and impeachment pressure alarmed Sieyès, whose executive project required containing the Jacobins. Schérer faced corruption accusations alongside the former Directors; after campaigning, eviction and Fouché’s closure of the Manège, the Five Hundred rejected the indictments.
Jourdan’s Country in Danger motion threatened renewed extraordinary powers and evoked fears of1793; its defeat before the later military successes marked the limit of Jacobin emergency influence.

source_treatments.label: Jacobins under the Directory: revival, controlled mobilization, and repression
source_treatments.meaning: In 1795–1796 official indulgence and subsidies aided the press and Pantheon Club before closures and purges forced radicals underground. After Fructidor the constitutional circles rallied anti-royalists, then again faced restriction when demands for democracy and wider suffrage escaped government control.
source_treatments.stance: The two cycles illustrate tactical use without empowerment of the left. Neither Jacobins nor constitutional circles were a uniform organization; distinguish Babouvist conspiracy, broad republican mobilization, and later parliamentary ambitions.

source_treatments.label: Jacobin resurgence and emergency politics in 1799
source_treatments.meaning: The post-Prairial revival of Jacobin newspapers, clubs, officeholding, and emergency legislation during renewed military danger, followed by Sieyes's containment of the movement. Jacobin efforts to impeach the former Directors and General Schérer rested on accusations of corruption; the indictments were ultimately rejected, not established as judicial findings.
source_treatments.stance: The resurgence was real but did not command a parliamentary majority. Wartime emergency and memories of Year II magnified fear; Sieyes’s containment served his own executive project. Rejection of Jourdan’s Country in Danger motion marks the limit of renewed emergency government.

subjects.label: Directory: political balance, loss of legitimacy and collapse
subjects.meaning: The Directory sought a propertied republican centre between royalism and Jacobinism but alternated cultivation and repression, manipulated elections and relied increasingly on soldiers. Fiscal reconstruction alienated its intended supporters. It failed to organize its own moderate party or recognize legitimate opposition, while royalist restorationism and Jacobin associations with the YearII also obstructed compromise. Renewed war, religious coercion and conscription returned unresolved conflicts; popular abstention and silence concealed loss of confidence rather than stable consent. Constitutional failure arose from political practice and intolerance as well as institutional tensions. Belief that all honest citizens shared one general will made organized parties appear illegitimate factions, an ideological obstacle to accepting representative competition.
subjects.stance: The constitution was not simply doomed by design: political actors refused to let it operate freely. Threats from both extremes were real, but repeated preemption destroyed trust and abstention cannot be read as positive consent.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Convention frames the new regime as a stable republican settlement designed to block both terrorism and royalism.
The founding regime alternately restrained Jacobins or royalists according to which threat appeared greater.
The regime dismantled autonomous Parisian machinery and relied on troops; limited repression after Vendémiaire sought to regain propertied support rather than renew Terror.
Fructidor is judged to have destroyed the constitution's first real test and inaugurated a regime willing to set aside inconvenient results.
Fiscal recovery and bankruptcy alienated the propertied groups on which the regime sought to rely.
Floréal perpetuates executive control by denying the electorate's choices for a second time in a year.

Conscription, renewed war, anti-clerical coercion and unsettled authority bring the Revolution full circle; the conclusion anticipates future military abandonment rather than narrating a completed coup.

Coup leaders blamed constitutional weakness, though Directors had dominated legislatures through manipulation. Sieyes sought a rationally redesigned constitution; Bonaparte sought effective personal power, distinct remedies for the failing regime.

Discounted elections and abstention undermined legitimacy. Belief in one honest general will delegitimized parties, and Directors failed to organize a moderate center; royalist restoration aims and Jacobin associations with the Year II also made opposition threatening, continuing on 377.
Royalists and Jacobins also rejected compromise and the legitimate interests of opponents, making the crisis more political than constitutional.
The conclusion anticipates the army abandoning a government that has failed to settle the conflicts sustaining war and coercion.

source_treatments.label: Directory, political character and instability, 1795-1799
source_treatments.meaning: The Directory as a property-based republican middle way that sought stability between Jacobinism and royalism but repeatedly overrode constitutional government and became dependent on military power.
source_treatments.stance: The regime alternately cultivated and repressed left and right, seeking a propertied republican middle way. Its coups expressed failure to trust its constitution; fiscal reconstruction alienated its intended supporters. Renewed war, religious coercion, and conscription recalled earlier revolutionary conflicts without making the Directory identical to the Year II.

source_treatments.label: Failure of the Directory, Constitution of Year III, and representative politics
source_treatments.meaning: The chapter's structural explanation for the Directory's collapse: repeated electoral manipulation, mistrust of voters, rejection of party politics, and irreconcilable royalist and Jacobin opposition.
source_treatments.stance: The constitution was not given a genuine trial: political manipulation and rejection of legitimate organized opposition destroyed its credibility. The Directors failed to organize their own centre and alternately suppressed parties. Yet royalist and Jacobin threats were real; critique of repression is not proof that either extreme would tolerate pluralism.

subjects.label: Sister republics: creation, constitutional diversity and constrained sovereignty
subjects.meaning: French-sponsored republics varied in constitutional authorship and domestic autonomy. Dutch elected life and locally drafted Ligurian institutions differed from imposed Swiss unity, Bonaparte’s dictated Cisalpine constitution and initial nominees, and the Roman commandant’s explicit supremacy. Local reformers and French military or anti-clerical initiatives interacted; occupation, strategic access, fiscal obligations and repeated coups limited sovereignty. The Directory did not welcome every new satellite: Championnet’s independent Neapolitan creation depended on French troops and collapsed when they withdrew.
subjects.stance: Do not flatten Dutch or Ligurian local initiative into the same model as imposed Swiss unity or Roman military supremacy. The Directory did not uniformly welcome every new satellite, but their spread deepened international alarm.

evidence.evidence_summary: French-backed Swiss intervention and a Roman riot killing a French general supplied openings for new republics; anti-clerical Directors and ambitious commanders encouraged expansion, military access and papal captivity.
Championnet proclaims the Parthenopean Republic despite the Directory's reluctance to assume another rootless puppet state.
The Batavian Republic is introduced as the first sister republic and the only conquered region with common revolutionary sympathizers.
The Helvetic constitution was imposed without ratification and secured permanent French military access.

The Ligurian constitution was drafted locally and approved by plebiscite. Roman institutions instead came from Parisian jurists, operated initially through nominees and required the French commandant’s consent, with independent lawmaking power reserved to him.

Championnet created the Parthenopean Republic despite Directorial reluctance, then was recalled after defying a civil commissioner. Withdrawal of French forces against renewed northern threats left the dependent regime exposed and it collapsed.

French pressure and a purge enabled a unitary Batavian constitution with a popularly elected bicameral legislature choosing five Directors; democratic provisions coexisted with coercion against opponents.

evidence.evidence_summary: After Daendels’s coup removed self-perpetuating rulers, elections began functioning regularly until renewed Parisian intervention in1800.

source_treatments.meaning: French creation or sponsorship of the Helvetic, Roman, and Parthenopean republics as instruments and consequences of expansion.
source_treatments.stance: The republics are presented as imposed, dependent, and often unstable; the Directory did not uniformly welcome every new puppet regime, but their creation deepened international alarm.

source_treatments.label: Sister republics as dependent French client states
source_treatments.meaning: The Batavian, Helvetic, Cisalpine, Ligurian, Roman, and Parthenopean republics as constitutional experiments constrained by French strategic and fiscal priorities.
source_treatments.stance: Client institutions varied substantially: Dutch elections and relative domestic autonomy, locally drafted Ligurian institutions, imposed Swiss unity, and the Roman commandant’s explicit supremacy must not be flattened into identical puppets. Military dependence and French interference qualified all these experiments.

subjects.label: Great Nation: territorial expansion, liberation claims and coercive hegemony
subjects.meaning: Continental victory and post-Floréal confidence encouraged the Great Nation’s claim to superior liberty, natural frontiers and entitlement to follow its own rules. Belgium’s occupation and annexation contrasted with dependent Italian republics; nominally republican institutions could conceal appointed rulers and military supremacy. Extraction, religious coercion and disregard of foreign traditions turned deference into resistance and helped renew coalition war. Foreign collaborators and reforms remained real, but support diminished; the1799 military reversal destroyed the Italian client system, not every sister republic everywhere.
subjects.stance: The source criticizes nationally exclusive liberty and arrogance while recognizing institutional changes and native collaborators. Territorial form and degrees of control differed; loss of legitimacy was not proof that every reform had no value.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Directory’s post-Floréal confidence was squandered most fatefully in foreign affairs, where the Great Nation claimed superiority and freedom to act by its own rules.
Claims of natural frontiers and exceptional entitlement accompanied browbeaten Rastadt concessions, secularization and Swiss/Italian interventions; deferential responses reinforced French arrogance.
Expansion and the Egyptian invasion alarm multiple powers and help create a renewed coalition.
The author contrasts French definitions of liberty with Dutch and Swiss traditions, framing the incompatibility between national French power and other peoples’ political freedoms.

Foreign support dwindled as hostility expanded. Renewed coalition war overwhelmed French resources inItaly, where sister republics collapsed amid reprisals; the passage does not say allclientstateselsewhere vanished.
Rhineland experience made French claims of freedom appear linguistically inverted to populations subjected to occupation and anticlerical coercion.

source_treatments.label: Occupied Europe under revolutionary French rule, 1794-1799
source_treatments.meaning: The chapter-wide transformation of conquered or coerced European territories through annexation, military occupation, and dependent republican regimes.
source_treatments.stance: Annexations, occupations and dependent republics took different constitutional forms. French liberty increasingly meant French national control, unable to accommodate other traditions of freedom. Extraction and intervention reduced foreign support and multiplied enemies; this is a qualified argument about domination, not a claim that all reform or native cooperation was absent.

subjects.label: War finance through conquest: extraction, army dependence and occupied economies
subjects.meaning: French armies and government relied on foreign coin, requisitions, indemnities, seized treasuries and art, trade restrictions and client-funded forces. These systemic demands strengthened commanders and burdened occupied societies; Belgium’s Agency for Trade and Extraction exemplified organized removal. Dutch losses combined British blockade and colonial warfare with French occupation costs and discriminatory tariffs. Effects varied: after earlier Belgian exploitation, urban industry benefited from French market access in calmer years, while rural hostility persisted.
subjects.stance: Extraction was a state and military system, not merely private misconduct, and foreign coin did not solve France’s fiscal crisis. Distinguish French demands from Britain’s blockade, and immediate or persistent costs from the specific later Belgian industrial recovery; no universal recovery or permanent-impoverishment claim follows.

evidence.evidence_summary: Batavian payments and large sums taken from Germany and Italy become the chief source of coin, underscoring dependence on generals.
Dutch trade, industry, employment, and poor relief deteriorated under war, blockade, occupation costs, and discriminatory French tariffs.
Belgium was subjected to war taxes, requisitions, cash levies, and an Agency for Trade and Extraction before annexation.
The Rhineland was repeatedly stripped to support armies the French government could not pay.
Swiss treasuries were seized, war taxes imposed, and pillaging only sporadically controlled.
Italian war taxes, requisitions, impounded treasuries, art seizures, and bullion transfers financed the army and France.
French demands and forced political interventions in Liguria, Cisalpina, and Rome reinforced the satellites' dependency.
Belgian urban industry gained profitable access to the French market in calmer years despite prior rapine and higher taxes; rural resistance and estrangement persisted.

subjects.label: Jourdan Law: conscription, institutionalization and resistance
subjects.meaning: The Jourdan Law of1798 established annual classes of citizens aged twenty to twenty-five available for defense when volunteers were insufficient. Full activation in1799 called eligible men in those classes and prohibited purchased substitutes, meeting military need while provoking evasion, desertion, royalist recruitment and banditry. Pressure continued beyondBrumaire and eased with peace.
subjects.stance: Recruitment answered military need while reviving memories of coercive mobilization. It was not one of the civil measures repealed after Brumaire: keep it separate from the forced loan and hostage law.

evidence.evidence_summary: With the army reduced to 270,000, the law revives the levée en masse principle and creates annual classes subject to draft.
The text links renewed conscription to the earlier Vendée uprising and to the Revolution's return to coercion and instability.
The Councils activated the call of eligible twenty-to-twenty-five-year-olds, prohibiting purchase of substitutes and presenting it as a renewed mass levy.
Conscription refugees swell the planned royalist peasant force in the south-west.
A sweeping conscription measure helps trigger renewed chouannerie in the west.
Flight from recruiting officers contributes to endemic banditry until peace eases the pressure.

source_treatments.label: Jourdan Law and conscription, 1798
source_treatments.meaning: The law making citizens available for national defense and authorizing annual drafts of men aged twenty to twenty-five when volunteers were insufficient.
source_treatments.stance: Presented as a necessary response to depleted armies and renewed coalition war, but also as a return to coercive revolutionary patterns associated with the Vendée and civil conflict.

source_treatments.label: Jourdan conscription law and the renewed levee en masse
source_treatments.meaning: Full activation of the Jourdan law conscripted men aged twenty to twenty-five without substitution, supplying armies but provoking resistance, desertion, and royalist recruitment.
source_treatments.stance: The measure answered military necessity yet revived Year II associations and helped destabilize the countryside.

subjects.label: Bonaparte’s departure from Egypt, return and coup alliance
subjects.meaning: News of European disasters and the failing Egyptian prospect led Bonaparte to leave his army without waiting for the Directory’s order. His acclaimed return made him the available military partner in a coalition with Sieyes, Lucien, Fouché and Talleyrand.
subjects.stance: Prestige concealed abandonment and allowed different factions to project hopes onto him. Sieyes underestimated Bonaparte’s independent political ambition; the return prepared but did not itself accomplish Brumaire.

evidence.evidence_summary: Delayed news of European defeats and pessimism aboutEgypt led Bonaparte to depart secretly before receiving the already-issued evacuation order. The army he left later surrendered two years afterward, then depleted by two-thirds; thatlaterloss is not assigned wholly tohisdeparture.

subjects.label: Concordat: negotiated settlement, papal revival and lasting polarization
subjects.meaning: Bonaparte and PiusVII negotiated restoration of public Catholic worship and a paid, reorganized hierarchy, recognizing Catholicism as the majority faith while preserving freedom of belief and worship. Government nominated bishops, the Pope conferred spiritual authority, and clergy swore obedience to the state. Alienated Church lands were not returned, though the Pope did not concede the legality of confiscation or Avignon’s annexation. A renewed episcopate and papal authority defeated both full old-regime restoration and complete separation. Unilateral Organic Articles then restricted papal communication beyond the agreed bargain. Papal revival coexisted with material loss and enduring Catholic–republican polarization.
subjects.stance: The settlement was a difficult compromise, not old-regime restoration or a simple French diktat. It reconciled major institutions without erasing every religious division, and the papacy’s gain coexisted with Gallican restrictions and eventual political separation.

subjects.label: Elections of 1789: rules, mobilization and composition of the orders
subjects.meaning: The 1789 elections used inherited bailliages and senechaussees, grouped districts, separately represented towns and provincial exceptions, with different rules for each order. Broad male-taxpayer primary participation led through indirect stages whose cost, leisure and professional demands filtered out peasants and artisans; turnout remained limited despite unprecedented mobilization. Government largely avoided direct management, but its institutional design favoured parish priests and petty nobles and excluded incomplete ennoblements. Clerical deputies sought stipends, advancement and synods yet shared deeper commitments to Catholic authority, education, censorship and limited toleration. Noble delegates displaced court and robe leaders, largely accepted fiscal equality but divided over voting and political accommodation; Breton nobles boycotted. Third-estate deputies were chiefly lawyers and officeholders whose shared legal culture, head-voting demands and civil/fiscal equality produced unusual cohesion. The royal regulations established constituencies, order assemblies, franchise rules, indirect voting, deputy ratios, and cahier production. Ancient northern and southern judicial jurisdictions, sometimes grouped or supplemented, formed the principal national electoral geography. Provinces with surviving or newly restored estates received different electoral treatment, especially Dauphine, Navarre, and Brittany. Male taxpayers over twenty-five could enter primary assemblies, but delegates and final deputies were selected through successive indirect stages. Peasants and artisans could enter some primary assemblies but did not survive the indirect process into the final delegation. Ministers largely avoided direct management of electoral outcomes, but the rules they issued reshaped representation in every order. The elections drew unprecedented numbers into public affairs but turnout varied and was limited even in Paris. The electoral and cahier process extended public deliberation across France on a scale unmatched in contemporary Europe. Electoral rules produced a first-estate delegation dominated by parish priests rather than bishops and corporate hierarchy. Clergy across internal ranks shared commitments to stronger Church authority, education control, censorship, and limited Protestant toleration. Noble elections displaced some expected leaders, produced conflicts among court, robe, provincial, and local elites, and yielded a fragmented delegation. Noble grievance lists showed near unanimity on surrendering fiscal privilege but no comparable consensus on political voting or the basis of nobility. After election a reform minority sought accommodation with third-estate equality, while a larger bloc resisted common procedure. The final third-estate contingent was socially and professionally homogeneous, dominated by lawyers and officeholders rather than producers or laborers. Shared legal-cultural background and commitments to head voting plus civil and fiscal equality made third-estate deputies unusually cohesive.
subjects.stance: Distinguish formal eligibility from effective representation, overt noninterference from neutrality of rules, and parliamentary or clerical reform from wholesale ideological agreement. Internal noble divisions crossed social strata; clerical solidarity could outlast parish grievances, while the homogeneous Third delegation did not represent the social composition of the whole third estate. The source presents the regulations as enabling extraordinary participation while also shaping outcomes through unequal social and institutional filters. The chapter treats the districts as pragmatic inherited units whose exceptions mattered to representation. The author presents exceptions as politically contingent responses rather than a coherent federal principle. The source balances the breadth of formal eligibility against the strong social narrowing produced by time, expense, and professional competence. The chapter distinguishes formal primary inclusion from effective exclusion at the stage where deputies were selected. The author distinguishes absence of overt manipulation from neutrality of institutional design. The chapter rejects both a simple democratic triumph narrative and a dismissal of the elections as socially closed. The chapter calls the spectacle extraordinarily democratic while preserving its indirect structure, unequal order rules, abstention, and social exclusions. The chapter treats lower-clergy success as a real institutional defeat for hierarchy and a basis for later defections, while warning against assuming complete patriotic alignment. The author cautions that excitement over parish-priest reform obscured solidarities more durable than the order's immediate representation dispute. The author rejects the image of a monolithic, confident nobility and emphasizes organizational weakness beneath wealth and status. The chapter uses the cahiers to demonstrate genuine reform willingness alongside constitutional fragmentation. The author treats both camps as socially diverse and the division as political rather than a simple rich-poor split. The author treats this composition as the outcome of electoral filters and relevant skills, not as proof that the third estate at large shared the deputies' social position. The source contrasts their unity with the other orders while avoiding the claim that all deputies arrived nationally famous or socially representative.

subjects.label: Formation of the National Assembly and the Tennis Court Oath
subjects.meaning: After hesitant negotiations and an invitation to common verification, legally trained deputies deliberately crossed precedent by unilateral roll-call and adopted the National Assembly title. Existing taxes were declared unlawful but provisionally authorized only while the Assembly continued to sit, asserting fiscal sovereignty. Preparations for a Royal Session left the meeting hall locked; deputies interpreted this as threatened dissolution and swore not to disperse before creating a constitution. Clerical compromise efforts, conscience-based hesitation and gradual defections, followed by noble accessions and compelled union, widened the national claim. Sieyes moved a last invitation to the other orders followed by unilateral verification if they refused. Legally trained deputies delayed breaking precedent, recognized the irrevocability of unilateral action, and used formal verification and resolutions to construct new authority. The verified representatives adopted a national title and ceased to define themselves as one corporate order. The Assembly declared existing taxes unlawful yet provisionally valid while it continued to sit. Bailly combined scientific reputation with third-estate election and early procedural leadership as president of the Commons. Sovereignty shifted from royal authorization toward a representative Assembly claiming authority in the name of the nation. Secretive preparation for a royal intervention left deputies facing locked doors and soldiers on 20 June. Deputies pledged not to disperse until a constitution and public regeneration were secured. The emerging National Assembly claimed a mission to create a constitution and regenerate public authority. Clergy, nobility, and third estate were both social orders and competing constitutional bodies whose separate or common representation determined national legitimacy. The first estate combined narrow procedural votes for separation with sustained hesitation, conscience-based conciliation, and growing defections to common verification. Clerical and noble defections, popular pressure, and failed royal coercion compelled the formal merger of the remaining orders into the National Assembly.
subjects.stance: The rupture was reluctant and recognized as difficult to reverse. Distinguish the actual purpose of the hall closure from deputies’ fears, the Assembly’s legal claims from later popular/military enforcement, and gradual clerical realignment from an initially united reform bloc. Bailly’s presidency is substantive; his brief scientific background is contextual. The author identifies the ensuing roll-call as the start of the true revolutionary struggle because deputies knowingly took national legality into their own hands. The author presents the rupture as deliberate and reluctant rather than spontaneous lawlessness. The author treats the declaration as the institutional conversion of representation into sovereignty, not a merely verbal change. The author treats the resolution as an unmistakable sovereign claim because dissolution would authorize fiscal disobedience. The source gives him a defined institutional role but does not yet analyze the later mayoral career that begins outside this chunk. The chapter traces an effective, contested transfer: declaration and fiscal action asserted sovereignty, popular and military developments made it enforceable, and royal retreat confirmed it. The chapter emphasizes that poor notification and coercive appearances converted even opponents of 17 June into defenders of the Assembly's right to meet. The oath is presented as a deliberate collective response to apparent royal obstruction that bound the Assembly to a constituent mission. The source shows this constituent purpose developing from representation and verification rather than existing fully formed at the chapter's outset. The chapter shows that numerical representation, verification, deliberation, and voting could not be separated from the orders' conflicting claims. The chapter treats lower-clergy crossings as decisive but gradual, reflecting both institutional solidarity and pressure from public events. The author treats union as a victory for national representation but not the end of popular or Court conflict.

subjects.label: Paris uprising and the storming of the Bastille,12–14 July 1789
subjects.meaning: The Paris uprising of 12–14 July joined reaction to Necker’s dismissal and cavalry action with food fears, attacks on customs barriers, grain discovery at Saint-Lazare and a propertied militia initially unable to control crowds. Arms taken from the Invalides, failed negotiation, garrison fire and the French Guards’ cannon expertise led to the Bastille’s surrender. Militia formation, troop fraternization and armed July action protected the Assembly and constrained royal choices. Armed crowds destroyed tax barriers and sections of the customs wall after Necker's dismissal. Armed crowds looted the monastery after finding stored grain during a search for weapons and suspected hoarding. Paris crowds acquired muskets and cannon from the veterans' hospital before moving on the Bastille. July food fears, militia formation, popular arming and the capture of the Bastille defeated Court counteraction. Armed crowds, failed negotiation, garrison fire, French Guards' expertise, and cannon pressure produced the fortress's surrender. Broglie’s assessment concerned the reliability of the wider army, not only the French Guards.
subjects.stance: Keep Bastille access explicit within the uprising. The prison’s weak defences were not known in advance; crowd initiative and military expertise both mattered. Earlier print campaigns and national mobilization are antecedents with their own requirements. The attacks link subsistence anger, fiscal resentment, and political revolt rather than serving as mere background vandalism. The incident is treated as a revealing convergence of subsistence fear, sacrilege, and anti-clerical suspicion, not a central institutional campaign. The episode matters as the material step that made the supposedly formidable fortress vulnerable to trained attackers. The author explains the event materially and politically, treating it as the climax that broke royal coercion rather than as an inexplicable symbolic eruption.

subjects.label: Burke’s Reflections: inherited order, conspiracy and revolutionary predictions
subjects.meaning: Burke opposed abstract rights and sudden constitutional reconstruction through an account of inherited institutions, property and social order. He attributed revolutionary destruction to intellectual and financial conspirators and predicted military domination. His criticism linked confiscation of Church land, paper currency and ecclesiastical reconstruction to the destruction of inherited order.
subjects.stance: Burke’s arguments are influential polemic attributed to him, not Doyle’s endorsement of either the old regime or a French conspiracy. The source records his predictions of provincial disintegration, currency collapse and military rule without here explicitly adjudicating their later accuracy.

subjects.label: Lille negotiations, Fructidor, and the hardening of French peace terms
subjects.meaning: British peace efforts developed from the failed 1796 mission to Lille in 1797 as Pitt adapted to allied defeats and strategic stalemate. Britain accepted French European gains but rejected uncompensated restitution of Dutch and Spanish colonial captures as well as French possessions.

subjects.label: Levy of 300,000 and resistance to conscription
subjects.meaning: The February 1793 levy of 300,000 used departmental quotas and, where volunteers failed, conscription by lot. subjects.label: Levée en masse and Carnot’s organization
subjects.meaning: The August 1793 levée requisitioned people and resources for war: unmarried men aged 18–25 entered military service, others supplied manufacture, food and transport, women made clothing and served hospitals, children made bandages and older men promoted public morale. Carnot helped translate the decree into military recovery, but nominal army strength exceeded trained and equipped forces and actual conscription fell short of radical universal-enlistment hopes.

subjects.label: Free people of colour: colonial citizenship and successive rights decisions
subjects.meaning: White opposition to colonial representation and violent repression, including Vincent Ogé’s execution, forced successive French assemblies to address free-coloured citizenship. Robespierre’s victory over Barnave enhanced his metropolitan standing. subjects.label: France—overlapping administrative, judicial, and ecclesiastical divisions
subjects.meaning: Provinces, generalities, intendancies, parlementary ressorts, archiepiscopal provinces, and dioceses overlapped and generated recurrent jurisdictional conflict. Provinces, generalities, parlementary ressorts, dioceses, and local jurisdictions overlapped because the Crown accumulated and adapted inherited institutions rather than imposing uniform structures. Ancient, unequal provinces and largely honorary governors coexisted with newer, more uniform generalities administered by intendants. The Church divided France into archiepiscopal provinces and dioceses whose boundaries and jurisdictional enclaves followed another nonuniform geography.
subjects.stance: The pattern was uneven and illogical in appearance, yet historically rooted and central to how the kingdom functioned. Treat fragmentation as historically rooted and partly functional, not merely irrational disorder. Preserve the distinction between provincial identity and operative royal administration. Treat ecclesiastical geography as an additional layer of jurisdictional pluralism.

subjects.label: France—legal, fiscal, and commercial fragmentation
subjects.meaning: Customary and Roman law, weights and measures, direct taxes, the gabelle, tolls, and internal customs varied sharply by locality. Written Roman law in much of the south and numerous northern customs produced district-level differences in marriage, inheritance, and property tenure. Direct and salt taxation varied sharply by province, tax base, and privilege, with northern and central France generally bearing heavier burdens. Nonuniform weights and measures and dense internal excise, toll, tariff, and customs barriers obstructed exchange and encouraged litigation and fraud fears.
subjects.stance: The fragmentation impeded exchange and invited fraud, litigation, and unequal burdens, although it often reflected geography, culture, and historical bargains. Do not imply a single law of France beyond limited royal edicts. Preserve regional and legal variation; do not portray every noble, province, or property type as taxed identically. Acknowledge both economic burden and roots in geography, culture, and historical rights.

subjects.label: French agriculture—low productivity and fragmented peasant property
subjects.meaning: Conservative technology, partible inheritance, morcellation, small ownership, and piecemeal leasing constrained productivity and marketable surplus. French farming was generally low-yield, conservative, and wasteful, and government-backed agrarian improvement discourse had little effect on ordinary practice. Partible inheritance repeatedly divided property, producing morcellation, small estates, and obstacles to compact management and capital-intensive farming. Millions of small owner-occupiers and widespread sharecropping organized cultivation in tiny, precarious units whose uncertain yields discouraged fixed rent.
subjects.stance: The author broadly accepts contemporary diagnoses of backwardness but explains the rational pressures behind small-scale cultivation and sharecropping. Treat backwardness as structural and uneven, not simply peasant ignorance or indolence. Treat legal inheritance as a root mechanism, while recognizing Church land as an exception. Present ownership and métayage as distinct tenure forms sharing small scale and insecurity.
acceptable_access: French agriculture—low productivity and fragmented peasant property

subjects.label: Agriculture—crop systems, fallow, and regional innovation
subjects.meaning: Dependence on grain, weak livestock and manure supplies, and extensive fallow limited yields, while maize, potatoes, and fodder rotations succeeded in particular regions. Fear of famine made grain for household subsistence a rational priority, limiting diversification and marketable surpluses. Peasant concentration on family grain supply reflected justified famine fear but limited diversification and marketable surplus. Maize and potatoes spread regionally after crises, but climate, fertilizer scarcity, livestock weakness, and extensive fallow limited diversification; Flemish rotations showed higher-yield alternatives.
subjects.stance: Innovation was possible where ecological shock or strong urban markets created incentives, but remained geographically restricted. Do not portray subsistence priorities as irrational; the source presents them as risk management with costly consequences. Preserve regional limits and avoid treating innovation as nationally available.

subjects.label: Commercial farming—Paris basin and gros fermiers
subjects.meaning: Urban demand around Paris and Flanders supported large leases, capital-intensive cultivation, and prosperous tenant farmers. High transport costs restricted wider market integration; even feasible improvements to roads, canals and tolls would not remove the basic national constraint on marketing surplus. Accessible urban demand supported exceptional large leaseholds and capitalized tenant farmers in the Paris basin, who accumulated land and challenged communal rights. High transport costs, regional markets, tolls, and the limits of road, river, and canal improvement constrained nationwide commercialization.

subjects.label: Poverty—scale, causes, and demographic pressure
subjects.meaning: Chronic underemployment, family dependency, population growth, and wages lagging prices left roughly a third of the population poor even in good times. subjects.label: Poor relief—ecclesiastical decline and public innovation
subjects.meaning: Traditional alms, hospitals and poor houses lost resources through restrictions on mortmain acquisition, weakened bequests, government debt measures and inflation. Lay philanthropy, masonic charity, depots de mendicite and charitable workshops tentatively supplemented ecclesiastical relief. Urban monasteries, hospitals, poorhouses, and private charity attracted migrants but became increasingly inadequate as claims grew and resources eroded. Masonic charity, philanthropic societies, dépôts de mendicité, and ateliers de charité represented tentative new lay and governmental responses to a feared crisis. Press, literary circles, learned societies and academies debated the crisis of poverty.
subjects.stance: Public concern and innovation grew, but resources remained inadequate to the scale of poverty. Wider agricultural, judicial and Church controversies are not independent obligations of this welfare requirement. Do not portray traditional provision as comprehensive even before its financial decline. Treat these as limited experiments rather than a national welfare system.

subjects.label: Poverty—begging, crime, prostitution, and abandoned children
subjects.meaning: The poor used begging, theft, smuggling, poaching, prostitution, and child abandonment as survival strategies under acute insecurity. Restricted work opportunities, dependency, pregnancy and loss of employment exposed women to prostitution and helped drive the abandonment of children into institutions with very high mortality. People without secure work used begging and a spectrum of illegal survival practices, generating elite fear of fraud, intimidation, and disorder. For poor women, especially dismissed and pregnant migrant servants, prostitution could become a desperate survival strategy leading to disease and further degradation. Child abandonment tripled as poverty grew; overwhelmed hospitals farmed infants to poor wet nurses, and most died before age five.
subjects.stance: Explain these practices materially rather than accepting elite assertions of moral depravity; retain described deception and coercion without erasing poverty, gender and family costs. Frame behavior as survival under precarity while preserving evidence of professional deception and coercion. Do not reduce prostitution to moral depravity; the source locates it in gendered economic vulnerability. Treat abandonment as evidence of economic incapacity rather than proof of lower-class moral decline.

subjects.label: Skilled work—guilds, journeymen and early factories
subjects.meaning: Apprenticeship, journeymanship and guild mastership organized skilled work, with small workshops predominant and access to mastership advantaging relatives without being uniformly closed. Illegal compagnonnages aided travelling journeymen with work, solidarity, collective action and sometimes conflict. Larger disciplined, guild-free factories remained exceptional. Training and legal guild organization structured skilled work through apprenticeship, journeymanship, mastership, fees, masterpieces, and craft regulation. Ménétra's tour de France illustrates journeymen's illegal but effective mutual-aid unions, labor organization, mobility, and inter-group violence. Large textile-printing, glass, and wallpaper works introduced exceptional scale, discipline, and guild-free organization into a world of small workshops.
subjects.stance: Distinguish master guilds from independent journeyman associations. Hierarchy coexisted with craft solidarity across master-worker divisions, particularly against merchants; factories were exceptions rather than the typical workplace. Avoid depicting guilds as simply closed: access was unequal but often not severely restricted, and mastership did not guarantee success. Treat Ménétra as a sustained illustrative case rather than a principal actor in the chapter. Treat factories as notable exceptions rather than evidence of generalized industrialization.

source_treatments.label: Skilled work—guilds, journeymen and early factories
source_treatments.meaning: Apprenticeship, journeymanship and guild mastership organized skilled work, with small workshops predominant and access to mastership advantaging relatives without being uniformly closed. Illegal compagnonnages aided travelling journeymen with work, solidarity, collective action and sometimes conflict. Larger disciplined, guild-free factories remained exceptional. Training and legal guild organization structured skilled work through apprenticeship, journeymanship, mastership, fees, masterpieces, and craft regulation. Ménétra's tour de France illustrates journeymen's illegal but effective mutual-aid unions, labor organization, mobility, and inter-group violence. Large textile-printing, glass, and wallpaper works introduced exceptional scale, discipline, and guild-free organization into a world of small workshops.
source_treatments.stance: Distinguish master guilds from independent journeyman associations. Avoid depicting guilds as simply closed: access was unequal but often not severely restricted, and mastership did not guarantee success. subjects.label: Industrial regulation and unrest under Louis XVI
subjects.meaning: Turgot’s 1776 attack on guild regulation was reversed; the 1781 livret tied workers to employer certification and strengthened control over mobility. Inflation, industrial discipline and unrest nevertheless coexisted with master-journeyman solidarity, especially against merchant direction in Lyons. A short-lived attempt to abolish guilds was followed by restoration and a work-record system that tightened employer control over labor mobility. Inflation, regulation, strikes, boycotts, and worker insubordination grew, but shared craft culture often united masters and journeymen against merchants and food-price shocks.
subjects.stance: Do not reduce the craft world to a uniform conflict between masters and workers; free trades, exceptional factories and collective craft interests qualified formal regulation. Preserve the reversal from apparent liberalization to renewed regulation. Do not reduce labor relations to a simple master-worker class conflict.

subjects.label: Bourgeoisie—growth, wealth, consumption, and culture
subjects.meaning: The bourgeoisie expanded faster than the population and controlled commercial, industrial, landed, officeholding and financial wealth. Its demand sustained urban building, luxury trades, education, theatres, print, reading rooms and associations; enrichment alongside growing poverty made inequality more visible. The bourgeoisie expanded faster than the population and controlled much commercial, industrial, landed, office, and financial wealth, forming most of the secure urban elite. Bourgeois demand sustained luxury trades, theatres, schools, colleges, books, newspapers, libraries, reading rooms, clubs, and cultural societies. Simultaneous growth of mass poverty and elite wealth made luxury more visible and sharpened resentment between secure elites and precarious majorities. Books, newspapers, reading rooms, clubs and cultural societies expanded the social infrastructure of bourgeois cultural life.
subjects.stance: This internally unequal group was more than industrial entrepreneurs. Cultural resources and print demand do not demonstrate unified revolutionary politics or bourgeois authorship of every institutional controversy. Treat it as internally unequal and increasingly weighty, not a unified revolutionary class. Treat cultural expansion as evidence of resources and public presence, not automatic political radicalization. Preserve this as a contemporary diagnosis and chapter-level synthesis, not proof of inevitable revolution.

subjects.label: Venal offices and the professional bourgeoisie
subjects.meaning: The hereditary resale of public offices made government service a vast capital market and a preferred route from commerce into respectable professional life. Most provincial professionals sought modest hereditary comfort and respectability rather than exceptional fortunes; education, status sensitivity and sociability shaped their lives. Masonic lodges supplied ritual, diversion, ideals and charitable activity within this provincial professional setting. The Crown sold hereditary and transferable public functions, creating more than 70,000 offices that absorbed bourgeois capital and linked finance, administration, status, and law. Most lawyers, notaries, judges, and writers sought modest hereditary comfort rather than great fortunes, filling under-occupied provincial worlds of education and status sensitivity. Masonic lodges offered ideals, ritual, sociability, and charitable activity to educated urban people.
subjects.stance: Officeholding provided dignity and modest security more often than great profit, while embedding purchased status throughout the state and judiciary. Masonic participation is a limited sociability and philanthropy route here, not evidence of a revolutionary conspiracy. Treat venality as a central social institution, not merely corruption or a fiscal expedient. Do not generalize exceptional professional success to the group as a whole. The chapter treats masonry as diversion and philanthropy, not a revolutionary conspiracy.

subjects.label: Ennoblement and bourgeois social mobility
subjects.meaning: Purchased offices, especially King's Secretaryships, enabled thousands of affluent commoners to enter the nobility and made ennoblement the summit of bourgeois success. Legitimate office purchase and petitions coexisted with fabricated ancestry, assumed titles and informal claims to noble standing. Thousands entered nobility through venal office, especially immediate ennoblement as King's Secretary, while others petitioned, forged genealogy, or adopted noble-sounding names.
subjects.stance: Mobility was substantial but strongly tilted toward wealth, provoking resentment among professional bourgeois and established nobles alike. Wealth-mediated mobility was substantial but did not create unrestricted social equality. Present ennoblement as substantial and accessible to wealth but still unequal and contested.

subjects.label: Bourgeois-noble tensions and barriers to public careers
subjects.meaning: Bourgeois-noble relations combined status resentment and barriers to careers with permeability through wealth, education, marriage and office purchase. The Segur Ordinance favoured poor hereditary nobles and professional military standards against rich recent entrants, while court privilege and its appearance of broad bourgeois exclusion complicated that purpose. Education, outlook, marriage, office, and wealth made the bourgeois-noble boundary permeable, yet both professional bourgeois and established nobles defended rank against moneyed parvenus and exclusion. Military schools and the 1781 ancestry requirement aimed to professionalize officers and support poor nobles but preserved privilege, excluded talent, and failed to restrain courtier amateurs.
subjects.stance: Distinguish intention, public reception and effects. Established education and social connections could cross order boundaries, while experienced lower-rank officers still faced obstacles; the policy was not simply a uniform ban on the whole bourgeoisie. Reject a rigid caste opposition without minimizing resentment and formal barriers. Preserve the reformers' professional aim and the author's critique of birth and wealth crowding out merit.

subjects.label: French navy—professional competence, conscription, and expansion
subjects.meaning: The navy combined more technical professional competence with red and blue officer routes, continuing noble preference, absence of purchased commissions and the classes reserve system for seamen. Expansion helped secure American independence but naval costs and the Cherbourg works added to fiscal exhaustion. Noble naval schools supplied 'red' officers, wartime maritime society supplied 'blues,' and registered naval classes mobilized experienced coastal labor, making competence more important than in the army. Post-1763 naval expansion produced wartime success and helped secure American independence, but sustained fleet and Cherbourg spending contributed to bankruptcy. Naval costs multiplied during the American war, while later defence spending and Cherbourg intensified fiscal strain.
subjects.stance: Compare these recruitment and advancement institutions with the army without treating naval service as socially equal. Naval expenditure is a specific fiscal contribution, not the entire monarchy-wide finance dossier. Preserve noble preference without claiming complete noble monopoly or social equality at sea. subjects.label: Clergy and Church—first estate, wealth, and tax privilege
subjects.meaning: The clergy formed the first estate, dominated worship and welfare institutions, owned extensive land and tithes, and defended exemption through representative organization and negotiated contributions. Regular and secular clergy differed in numbers, employment, local presence and resources. The Assembly of Clergy and General Agency managed corporate finance through free gifts and borrowing; parish clergy bore a disproportionate share of the burden. The First Estate included large regular orders, canons, and a minority of parish priests, unevenly distributed; ecclesiastical institutions dominated many townscapes and local economies. The Church held about a tenth of the land, levied uneven tithes, defended ordinary-tax exemption, and used its Assembly, Agency, free gift, internal levies, and credit to negotiate state contributions. Old Regime society distributed rights and exemptions through corporations, towns, provinces, and legally distinct orders, with the nobility and clergy enjoying especially extensive status and fiscal advantages.
subjects.stance: Its institutional strength and wealth were real, but uneven distribution within the order left parish clergy carrying disproportionate burdens. Exemption from ordinary taxes did not mean no contribution, and institutional presence varied locally. Do not equate the clergy with parish priests or assume uniform regional presence. Distinguish tax exemption from zero contribution and preserve the low effective burden relative to revenue. Do not reduce privilege to a uniform caste system: exemptions were widespread, varied by place and body, and coexisted with substantial mobility into nobility.

subjects.label: Parlements—judicial, legislative, and political opposition
subjects.meaning: Parlements combined appellate and administrative jurisdiction with registration of laws, remonstrances, publicity, strikes and resignations. Religious conflicts and especially fiscal demands enlarged opposition and public controversy, provoking Louis XV’s 1766 assertion of undivided sovereignty. As final appellate courts, administrative authorities, and registrars of law, parlements used remonstrances, publicity, strikes, and delay to oppose policy, though the king retained the lit de justice. Religious and especially fiscal conflict expanded provincial parlementary opposition, mobilized public opinion, and provoked Louis XV's 1766 assertion of undivided sovereign power. Printed remonstrances widened parlementary appeals beyond confidential judicial channels. War costs, borrowing and taxation intensified conflict between Crown and parlements; wartime taxes could not readily be reduced.
subjects.stance: These were powerful courts, not elected legislatures or sovereign co-rulers. Their obstruction and publicity coexisted with the king’s claimed and exercised final power of lit de justice. Treat parlements as powerful courts and political actors, not elected legislatures or sovereign co-rulers. Preserve both the courts' obstruction and the ultimate legal supremacy claimed and exercised by the monarch.

subjects.label: Maupeou reform and restoration of the parlements
subjects.meaning: Maupeou exiled resistant magistrates, replaced venal offices and reorganized courts in 1771. Louis XVI reversed the settlement after Louis XV’s death, but restoration recovered neither the parlements’ former credibility nor confidence that monarchy respected legal restraints. Maupeou exiled resisting magistrates, abolished parlementary venality, reorganized subordinate courts, and remodeled provincial parlements but failed to secure public legitimacy before Louis XV died. Louis XVI restored the old courts to signal good intentions, but suppression and restoration had exposed parlementary weakness and royal capacity for despotism, destroying the prior atmosphere of political confidence. Louis XV asserted royal sovereignty and supported Maupeou’s judicial reconstruction; his death reopened the settlement. Government propaganda failed during Maupeou’s reform, and expected public confidence influenced restoration.
subjects.stance: Preserve the double damage to judicial and royal legitimacy. The predecessor context here concerns judicial policy and succession, not every territorial, military or court episode of the two reigns. Recognize rationalizing elements without accepting official claims or denying the reform's coercive, dispossessing character. Preserve the double damage to both courts and Crown; restoration did not return politics to its earlier state.

Financiers and tax farmers furnished liquidity and credit; contested collection and conspicuous court expenditure exposed structural weakness.

subjects.label: Versailles and the Court—patronage, dependence, and power
subjects.meaning: Versailles concentrated rank, costly display, royal rewards and privileged access in a court system that made nobles dependent on favour while giving courtiers influence over wealth and appointments. Louis XIV’s court domestication remained an inheritance, modified by eighteenth-century noble recovery of major offices; successive favourites and ministers illustrate the operation of patronage. Versailles consumed major revenue, supported a dependent town and palace population, ranked courtiers by ancestry and presentation, and concentrated the kingdom's wealthiest, most influential noble elite. Royal favor allocated pensions, sinecures, office, and influence; favorites and mistresses could enrich families and make or break ministers. The young Austrian queen sought pleasure and favor for associates, resented the unconsummated marriage, and already participated in court appointment pressure without yet possessing mature political direction. Louis XV’s favouritism and mistresses influenced ministerial careers and court patronage. Louis XIV’s domestication of nobles at court supplied a baseline later altered by noble recovery of elite government.
subjects.stance: Distinguish the patronage system from territorial expansion, army development and judicial sovereignty. Examples of favourites explain access and influence, not a claim that all government was reducible to mistresses. Preserve both relatively open physical access and highly exclusive true court status. Do not dismiss court intrigue as trivial: the memoir details concerned real wealth and power. Preserve the source's sharply critical characterization without projecting later revolutionary accusations backward.

subjects.label: Louis XVI—accession, character, and political inexperience
subjects.meaning: Louis XVI inherited the throne at twenty with education, devotion, duty and good intentions but little preparation, political confidence or strategic direction. Louis XV had failed to prepare his heir; the young queen and court appointment pressures formed the immediate setting of the new reign. The twenty-year-old king was educated, devout, dutiful, and well-intentioned but poorly prepared, insecure, unimpressive, and unlikely to master the intrigue surrounding the throne. The young Austrian queen sought pleasure and favor for associates, resented the unconsummated marriage, and already participated in court appointment pressure without yet possessing mature political direction. Louis XV failed to prepare his heir for kingship; this shaped the personal inheritance at accession. Louis XVI’s indecisive accession contrasted with Louis XIV’s decisive assumption of authority.
subjects.stance: Credit conscientious intentions while retaining political insecurity. Early marital and court tensions do not establish later revolutionary accusations; territorial conquest and army history belong to their own requirements. Avoid caricature: credit good intentions and duty while preserving the author's judgment of inadequate political mastery. subjects.label: French cultural prestige and language in eighteenth-century Europe
subjects.meaning: The legacy of Versailles and French court culture made French architecture, fashions, material culture, and especially the French language dominant markers of elite cultivation across much of Europe. A shared elite language made French political developments and printed debate accessible across Europe, multiplying transnational observation. Louis XIV's court, palace, gardens, architecture, furnishings, and fashions established a model copied by rulers and elites across eighteenth-century Europe. French became the preferred language of courts and cultivated society across much of Europe, enabling educated readers to follow French affairs and consume French print directly. By the 1770 s writers in Germany and Italy attacked their compatriots' deference to French language and culture, although the reaction remained limited.
subjects.stance: French cultural predominance remained powerful into the 1770 s, despite a still-limited backlash against imitation of an alien culture. Nascent nationalist resistance had not yet displaced French cultural and linguistic dominance. Treat cultural prestige as a durable political legacy of Louis XIV, not as proof that French dominance was uncontested or permanent. Preserve both the breadth of francophone culture and the chapter's link between linguistic access, informed judgment, and the spread of French ideas. Do not imply that backlash had already displaced French prestige; it marks an emerging countercurrent.

subjects.label: Expansion of the French-language periodical press
subjects.meaning: The French-language press expanded through semi-official newspapers, independent journals, clandestine Jansenist publication, foreign presses and local or daily papers. Linguet sustained oppositional journalism through imprisonment and publication beyond royal jurisdiction; his memoirs shaped the Bastille’s reputation. Foreign journals supplied informed opposition as well as conservative and radical outlooks. The number and variety of journals rose sharply during the eighteenth century, widening access to political, religious, learned, literary, and general news. Semi-official journals remained closely censored, but the multiplying press exceeded the government's capacity for comprehensive supervision. The Jansenist Nouvelles ecclésiastiques maintained a sustained critique of the established Church while repeatedly evading efforts to locate and suppress its presses. Linguet's Annales survived his imprisonment through surrogates, popularized his attack on arbitrary detention, and later operated from the Austrian Netherlands to escape French control. French-language journals printed in Holland, Avignon, Prussian territories, and independent Bouillon supplied detailed reporting and intellectual criticism beyond ordinary French jurisdiction. Political upheavals increased demand for news; foreign and domestic circulation rose, provincial centers acquired papers, and a daily Paris press reached an audience far larger than copy totals alone.
subjects.stance: Retain distinct channels, continuing selective repression and estimated readership. Extraterritorial publication was not uniformly radical, and imprisonment did not necessarily silence a journal. Treat expansion as a structural enlargement of the informed public, while retaining the fragility of many individual journals. Avoid portraying censorship as absent; the point is declining practical control amid continued legal authority and selective repression. Treat the journal as an organized political-religious intervention, not merely as a title in a list of periodicals. Preserve his unpredictability and personal notoriety; do not turn him into a consistent revolutionary ideologue. Do not equate all foreign journals with radicalism; their outlooks ranged from conservative to anticlerical and anti-authoritarian. Treat the reported readership as an estimate and the press as expanding, not universally accessible.

subjects.label: Literacy, reading access, and the social composition of the reading public
subjects.meaning: Rising literacy and shared-reading institutions widened access to print, but cost and education meant that the cultivated reading public was still dominated by urban nobles, clergy, and professional bourgeois groups. Basic literacy opened access to cheap traditional blue-library print but did not make sophisticated books and journals affordable. Subscription libraries, reading rooms and other fee-based institutions widened access unevenly; noble, clerical and professional readers outweighed merchants in cultivated readership. More than a third of the population could read and write, sustaining a market for cheap almanacs and traditional tales distributed by traveling hawkers. Journal subscriptions and books cost too much for most artisans, and even comfortable readers needed collective institutions to sustain broad access to current literature. Provincial subscription libraries and reading rooms lowered the cost of following literature and political news and sometimes added spaces for conversation. Readers of sophisticated print were chiefly nobles, clergy, lawyers, magistrates, administrators, officers, and other professional bourgeois, concentrated in towns and less strongly represented among merchants and manufacturers.
subjects.stance: Access broadened beyond individual purchasers without becoming socially democratic; merchants and manufacturers were comparatively less engaged than professional and administrative readers. Do not infer broad access to sophisticated Enlightenment print from basic literacy or popular-book consumption. Treat economic exclusion as a central limit on the numerical reach of enlightened opinion. Do not describe these institutions as socially universal; fees still selected a comparatively prosperous reading public. Avoid treating the bourgeoisie as a single uniformly enlightened class; occupation, education, residence, and disposable income mattered.

subjects.label: Education after the suppression of the Jesuits
subjects.meaning: The expulsion and dissolution of the Jesuits fragmented French elite education, while colleges retained classical and Catholic foundations but increasingly taught scientific and experimental approaches. Experimental and Newtonian instruction could supply habits of rational criticism and practical usefulness later applied to human institutions. The expulsion and dissolution of the Jesuits broke the uniformity of Catholic elite education, dispersed their colleges among varied successors, and left France without a kingdom-wide replacement system. Elite secondary education still centered on years of Latin and Roman culture, reinforced by Catholic orthodoxy, with only limited additions such as geography and French history. Advanced college courses spread the methods and findings of the scientific revolution, including Newtonian physics, behind a formally Aristotelian facade. Students trained to judge nature by demonstrable operation and useful results could extend the same standards to social and political institutions despite lessons in obedience and orthodoxy. Classical and Catholic curricula persisted alongside newer scientific instruction.
subjects.stance: Institutional disruption produced diversity rather than a coordinated national reform; Newtonian and empirical teaching coexisted with formal Aristotelian and religious orthodoxy. This was a possible intellectual pathway, not proof that every scientifically educated pupil became a reformer; classical and Catholic education persisted. Do not equate institutional disruption with educational collapse; the result was greater diversity, not simple disappearance. Do not portray the curriculum as wholly secularized or modernized before the Revolution. Preserve the coexistence of institutional tradition and substantive intellectual change. Treat this as an interpretive pathway and intellectual possibility, not a deterministic claim that scientific education made every student a reformer.

subjects.label: The Enlightenment as a program of rational criticism and practical improvement
subjects.meaning: Enlightenment writers addressed an unprecedentedly literate educated public with criticism, popularization, and claims that institutions should be judged by reason, usefulness, and human happiness. Shared persecution and common adversaries helped create a collective philosophic identity without doctrinal uniformity. The Enlightenment is defined as a movement of criticism that subjected institutions and beliefs to rational tests of improvement, usefulness, and contribution to human happiness. Enlightenment writers styled themselves independent thinkers committed to practical improvement and sought influence through polemic, simplification, and appeal to the educated public. Harassment by the Church and clerically influenced authorities helped disparate speculative writers recognize a shared movement and common cause. Mainstream enlightened thought treated material and intellectual progress as a winning struggle against superstition and as a force improving human welfare and institutions.
subjects.stance: The movement is presented as reformist, public-facing, and practically oriented rather than merely speculative, while containing internal disagreements and orthodoxies of its own. Progress and improvement were optimistic expectations contested within enlightened culture, not demonstrated universal laws. Preserve the movement's reformist and practical orientation without reducing its diversity to one doctrine. Do not confuse their activist self-conception with the older ideal of detached philosophical contemplation. Do not imply complete doctrinal unity; solidarity arose partly from common enemies and experiences of repression. Preserve the movement's optimism while noting shocks such as the Lisbon earthquake and the existence of dissenting positions.

subjects.label: The Encyclopédie and encyclopedism
subjects.meaning: Diderot and D'Alembert's Encyclopédie sought both to organize knowledge and to cultivate critical reflection, becoming a contested, widely distributed vehicle of independent thought. Malesherbes’s administrative protection helped the project survive repression. Diderot’s later radical thought extended beyond the early collective enterprise and beyond what contemporary readers knew of him. Diderot and D'Alembert transformed a translated reference project into a multi-author work intended both to organize knowledge and cultivate critical, philosophic reflection. Repeated attacks and suspension culminated in withdrawal of the Encyclopédie's privilege, but Malesherbes allowed publication to continue under tacit permission until completion. Expanded editions and smaller formats created a large market; notoriety, irreverence, and contempt for authority made the work influential, while encyclopedism came to signify independent judgment. Disillusioned with the Encyclopédie, Diderot moved toward political and economic radicalism while habits formed under censorship kept much of that development obscured from contemporaries.
subjects.stance: Censorship and notoriety enlarged its influence; its anti-authoritarian ethos was historically important, though encyclopedism also carried a confident orthodoxy of progress. Distinguish the project’s contemporary reputation from Diderot’s later or unpublished positions; censorship also generated publicity. Do not reduce the Encyclopédie either to a neutral reference work or to a simple revolutionary manifesto. Preserve the unstable combination of official repression, administrative protection, and continued production. Recognize both the work's reference quality and the anti-authoritarian reputation that chiefly drove sales. Do not infer that his public reputation in 1784 matched his later-recognized radical importance.

subjects.label: Rousseau's critique of progress, natural goodness, and legitimate authority
subjects.meaning: Rousseau argued that institutions and material progress could corrupt natural goodness. His novels and educational writing cultivated feeling and individual virtue, while the Social Contract theorized legitimate authority for small communities through a general will distinct from numerical majority. Later readers converted its formulas into a model of national regeneration. Rousseau rejected the orthodox claim that arts and sciences improved humanity, arguing instead that social institutions corrupted people who were naturally good. Julie and Émile used an emotionally direct style to dramatize innocence and virtue preserved against the corrupting snares of established society, winning a vast European readership. Rousseau's Social Contract offered a theoretical account of legitimate political authority compatible with natural liberty and warned that its model could function only in small city-states. Rousseau's infallible general will was not necessarily majority opinion, but common usage quickly simplified it into majority will and later revolutionaries treated it as part of a program for national regeneration. The religious passages of the Social Contract and Émile criticized clerical Christianity and affirmed a benevolent natural deity, provoking condemnation, an arrest decree, and exile.
subjects.stance: Literary morality is not a direct programme for wholesale social revolution. Civil and natural religion, including the Savoyard curate, prompted condemnation; Rousseau’s natural deity and criticism of clerical religion were not atheism. Treat his position as a foundational dissent within the Enlightenment, not as simple rejection of reason or all reform. Do not collapse these works into a political program; their primary treatment here concerns moral sentiment and social corruption. Do not present the work as a direct blueprint for wholesale French revolution or a program designed for a large monarchy. Preserve the distinction between Rousseau's qualified concept and its later political simplification. Preserve Rousseau's emotional religiosity; he appeared blasphemous to the devout but was not simply an atheist.

His emotional style and European impact are introduced.
The Social Contract theorized legitimate authority and natural liberty for small states; later revolutionary readers treated its general will as a practical guide beyond Rousseau's stated scope.
Julie and Émile are interpreted through innocence, virtue, and corrupt society.
The work's theoretical aim, liberty problem, and restriction to small city-states are explicitly distinguished from a program for change.
The concept's original qualification, rapid equation with majority will, and later revolutionary use are contrasted.
The condemned religious passages, arrest decree, flight, natural religion, and clerical critique are explained.

source_treatments.label: Rousseau's critique of progress, natural goodness, and legitimate authority
source_treatments.meaning: Rousseau argued that institutions and material progress could corrupt natural goodness. His novels and educational writing cultivated feeling and individual virtue, while the Social Contract theorized legitimate authority for small communities through a general will distinct from numerical majority. Later readers converted its formulas into a model of national regeneration. Rousseau rejected the orthodox claim that arts and sciences improved humanity, arguing instead that social institutions corrupted people who were naturally good. Julie and Émile used an emotionally direct style to dramatize innocence and virtue preserved against the corrupting snares of established society, winning a vast European readership. Rousseau's Social Contract offered a theoretical account of legitimate political authority compatible with natural liberty and warned that its model could function only in small city-states. Rousseau's infallible general will was not necessarily majority opinion, but common usage quickly simplified it into majority will and later revolutionaries treated it as part of a program for national regeneration. The religious passages of the Social Contract and Émile criticized clerical Christianity and affirmed a benevolent natural deity, provoking condemnation, an arrest decree, and exile.
source_treatments.stance: Literary morality is not a direct programme for wholesale social revolution. Civil and natural religion, including the Savoyard curate, prompted condemnation; Rousseau’s natural deity and criticism of clerical religion were not atheism. Treat his position as a foundational dissent within the Enlightenment, not as simple rejection of reason or all reform. Do not collapse these works into a political program; their primary treatment here concerns moral sentiment and social corruption. Do not present the work as a direct blueprint for wholesale French revolution or a program designed for a large monarchy. Preserve the distinction between Rousseau's qualified concept and its later political simplification. Preserve Rousseau's emotional religiosity; he appeared blasphemous to the devout but was not simply an atheist.
