subjects.label: Tax administration and indirect taxes under the Directory
subjects.meaning: The Agency for Direct Contributions centralized tax collection through departmental commissioners, experienced former fiscal staff and coercive billeting. The source groups restored levies on tobacco, traffic, legal documents, doors and windows as indirect taxation; salt tax did not return. Revenue recovery was slow and increased hostility among property holders.
subjects.stance: Presented as effective state rebuilding through methods and taxes reminiscent of the old regime, producing slow results and increased hostility among propertied citizens.

evidence.evidence_summary: The agency uses central commissioners, former fiscal personnel and billeting to enforce recovery; the text then groups tobacco, traffic, document, door and window levies as restored indirect taxation, without restoring salt tax.
Centralized taxation and indirect levies begin reconstruction but recovery is slow and politically costly.

subjects.label: Royalist organization and electoral strategy, 1796-1797
subjects.meaning: The turn from failed rebellion toward elections through the Clichy Club, right-wing press, Philanthropic Institutes, British support, and competing monarchist tendencies. The Philanthropic Institutes spread from Bordeaux as semi-secret electoral organizations; press campaigns exploited disorder and financial grievances. Louis-Philippe’s connection to a regicide father could attract constitutionalists. Gradualist hopes differed from Pichegru’s military conspiracy.
subjects.stance: Royalist cooperation was electoral and provisional: absolutists, constitutionalists and Orléanists did not share one settlement. Some institutes received British money, but a violent inner circle’s failed plot was not the whole movement. Blankenburg offered ambiguity, not clear acceptance of constitutional monarchy.

evidence.evidence_summary: With rebellion failing, royalists focus on the 1797 elections through Clichy and a well-funded press.

Absolutists, constitutionalists and Orléanists share provisional electoral work; Louis-Philippe’s regicide-parent association attracts some. The Bordeaux-origin Institutes spread nationally; press attacks target disorder and finance. Some British funding and Brottier’s failed inner conspiracy do not define the entire movement.

Blankenburg ambiguously reassures property holders without clearly repudiating Verona. Elected royalists range from gradual constitutional hopes to Pichegru’s established military contacts; official manoeuvres fail to secure the desired result.

subjects.label: Executive-legislative conflict, 1797
subjects.meaning: The confrontation between a divided Directory and the post-election Councils over peace, ministers, finance, refractory clergy, and military influence. Leoben raised hopes for a workable peace. Carnot and Barthélemy favoured accommodation, Barras initially wavered, while Reubell and La Revellière feared royalist success. Conflicts over ministers, finances, clergy and military interests made the executive’s own divisions central to escalation.
subjects.stance: The text presents a real possibility of cooperation with a moderate majority, but fear of royalist triumph and generals' hostility drove escalation toward Fructidor.

evidence.evidence_summary: Leoben encourages hopes for peace as the YearV results remove the Directors’ stable legislative support but leave a heterogeneous new majority.

Carnot and Barthélemy favour pragmatic cooperation, Barras wavers and Reubell/La Revellière resist. Peace, ministerial appointments, financial control, clergy and the generals’ conquest interests intensify the constitutional conflict.
The military coup resolves the conflict by purging the Councils rather than testing constitutional accommodation.
The author considers cooperation with a moderate republican majority more plausible than an immediate royalist takeover.
evidence.reconciliation_rationale: Retain this inspected final-release page claim in the named successor treatment; the chapter proposal used fewer illustrative pages,which is not grounds to lose this source-supported facet.

subjects.label: Directorial Terror after Fructidor
subjects.meaning: The months-long post-coup repression of émigrés, nobles, royalists, refractory clergy, and opposition institutions.
subjects.stance: Broad anti-royalist and anti-Catholic repression, described as Directorial Terror, did not duplicate the Year II’s scale or institutions. Preserve the difference between draconian legal liability and uneven implementation, especially the anti-noble citizenship law.

evidence.evidence_summary: Revived émigré laws expose returnees to execution. Categorical noble citizenship deprivation reaches regime supporters but is weakly or not enforced, unlike actual executions of some émigrés.
Clerical deportation, anti-Catholic policy, and selective mobilization of Jacobins extend the post-coup campaign.

subjects.label: Refractory priests and clerical deportation after Fructidor
subjects.meaning: Reactivation of laws against nonjuror clergy, the oath of hatred for royalty, and deportations to Ré, Oléron, and Guiana. Refusal was concentrated in annexed Belgium, where fear of resistance constrained enforcement; people liable, island internees and those actually shipped to Guiana were different populations.
subjects.stance: The repression is presented as a severe blow to the religious revival, but mass enforcement was constrained in annexed Belgium and actual transport to Guiana was limited.

evidence.evidence_summary: Refusal of the new anti-royalist oath makes priests liable to summary deportation as returned clergy face renewed persecution.

About10,000refuse the oath, mostly in annexed Belgium where authorities fear resistance to mass enforcement. Roughly1,400reach island depots but only about230Guiana; deaths in detention/transport do not equal all those legally liable.

subjects.label: Bonaparte and the Directory
subjects.meaning: Bonaparte's rising political importance as Vendémiaire artillery adviser, victorious general, provider of intelligence, supporter of Fructidor, and commander dispatched to Egypt. His partisan army addresses and defence of conquest backed the anti-Council executive without requiring his personal presence in Paris. The Directors thought either success in Egypt or failure discrediting him could serve their interests.
subjects.stance: The Directory needs his military power but fears his autonomy and prestige; sending him to Egypt serves both strategic hopes and the political wish to remove him from France.

evidence.evidence_summary: Bonaparte advises Barras during the military defeat of Vendémiaire.
Bonaparte mobilizes partisan army addresses, resists surrender of conquests, supplies Pichegru intelligence, threatens intervention and sends Augereau.
Bonaparte’s prestige and independent policy alarm the Directors; an Egyptian success might help France, while failure could discredit a politically awkward general abroad.
The Directory welcomes Egypt as an indirect strategic attack on Britain and a means of removing Bonaparte from domestic politics, whether he succeeds or is discredited.

subjects.label: Electoral abstention and political disengagement under the Directory
subjects.meaning: Persistent low participation, limited protest against annulled results, and the social conditions that made electoral manipulation easier.
subjects.stance: Low participation and weak protest facilitated manipulation, but were not positive consent to coups. Restored local autonomy and satisfaction with peace and victory also muted national resistance.

Little protest follows two coups because the electorate is largely disengaged, local autonomy has partly returned, and peace with victory is popular.

subjects.label: Directorial commissioners and official electioneering
subjects.meaning: The centrally appointed departmental commissioners and other local officials used to reshape administrations, direct electoral influence, and later collect taxes. Elected local administrations survived within a system of central surveillance; doubtful departments could be remodelled. This continuity with earlier revolutionary central agents underlay official middle-way electioneering and later fiscal collection.
subjects.stance: The network linked local government to Paris and enabled increasingly systematic interference, while also supplying the machinery for later fiscal centralization.

evidence.evidence_summary: Centrally appointed commissioners supervise elected departmental administrations, remodel doubtful authorities and promote middle-way republican candidates, preserving central oversight in a partly elective local system.
An anti-extremist electoral oath and restrictions on émigré voting supplemented official electioneering.
The same centralized local network is used by the new Agency for Direct Contributions.
Government officials monitor departments and encourage rival electoral assemblies to create grounds for deciding disputed results.

subjects.label: Religion, anticlerical policy, and resistance to French rule
subjects.meaning: The cross-regional role of church confiscation, clerical persecution, sacrilege, and threatened religious customs in generating resistance.
subjects.stance: Religious policy was a central and often self-defeating source of hostility, especially when coupled with conscription and economic burdens.

evidence.evidence_summary: Monastic dissolution, confiscation, civil registration, the anti-royalist oath, and clerical deportations alienated Belgium.

Swiss church nationalization and reform provoked Catholic districts that joined religion to inherited democratic freedoms.
Italian resistance treated French soldiers' church plunder, blasphemy, and contempt for religious practice as defining injuries.
Vive Maria movements and attacks on Jews show how religious and local conflicts shaped urban counterrevolution.

subjects.label: Second Coalition and the collapse of French power in 1799
subjects.meaning: The interaction of indigenous resistance with coalition warfare drove French armies back in 1799. Defeat at Stockach and retreat from Switzerland accompanied Suvorov’s advance in Italy, where by the end of June French forces were confined to a coastal strip around Genoa and the Italian sister republics collapsed amid revenge and reprisal.
subjects.stance: Coalition warfare and locally varied popular resistance reinforced one another. French offensives despite numerical inferiority ended in defeat and the collapse of Italian client regimes; Dutch and Swiss outcomes differed. Do not describe every revolt as caused by the coalition or treat hostility alone as a sufficient military explanation.

evidence.evidence_summary: The renewed war determined the fate of the increasingly unstable Italian sister republics.

Defeat at Stockach, retreat from Switzerland and Suvorov’s advance drove the French back; by the end of June they were confined around Genoa, and the Italian sister republics collapsed amid revenge and reprisal.

subjects.label: Irish Rebellion of 1798
subjects.meaning: The Irish rising’s planning, government pre-emption, regional outbreaks, British repression, defeat and casualties. Disarmament and arrests helped precipitate desperate action; localized armies lacked coordination and faced overwhelming force. Wexford’s sectarian panic and defeat at Vinegar Hill are an important regional phase.
subjects.stance: The rebellion had little realistic chance of success and never became the imagined British Vendée. Its exceptional pro-French character and destructive scale coexist with geographic fragmentation and incompatible political aims; preserve the source’s qualification that Poland might rival its size.
acceptable_access: Irish Rebellion--casualties and limited geographic spread

evidence.evidence_summary: Rural hardship, agrarian networks and expectations of renewed French intervention sustained preparations.

Arrests and failed Leinster/Ulster risings preceded unexpected sectarian panic in Wexford. Catholic bands massacred Protestants, but the rebel army failed to break out of the locality and was defeated by concentrated artillery at Vinegar Hill within weeks.
The revolt's scale, casualties, terrorizing effect, and incompatible participant aims are assessed.

subjects.label: Batavian Republic: constitutional reconstruction, 1795-1798
subjects.meaning: The prolonged replacement of the Dutch ancien régime by a unitary, representative Batavian constitution. Federalists defended inherited provincial autonomy while unitarians sought a centralized national constitution; their conflict produced deadlock before French-backed purges enabled a unitary outcome.
subjects.stance: A genuinely democratic project emerged from an existing representative tradition, after deadlock and French-backed coercion. Regular elections and relatively wide internal autonomy distinguish the Batavian case; these do not amount to independent foreign policy. The supplied page344 says “Two years” after conquest while its surrounding chronology runs from 1795 to 1798; do not infer a corrected elapsed interval.
acceptable_access: Guilds and established Church--Dutch constitutional reform
Batavian Republic--male suffrage and regular elections

evidence.evidence_summary: Patriots sought to replace the Union of Utrecht but split between Federalist provincial autonomy and a unitary national state, immobilizing the Convention elected in 1796.
The rejected 1797 draft, January 1798 purge, and approved 1798 constitution established a unitary republic.
After the June coup and elections, constitutional government functioned with regular elections until 1800.

subjects.label: French intervention and coups in the Batavian Republic
subjects.meaning: French orchestration or approval of Dutch purges and coups to resolve political impasse and curb successive factions. The French Fructidor coup provided an explicit model for breaking Batavian deadlock by purging opponents, followed in January 1798.
subjects.stance: France first supported a unitary purge and then accepted Daendels’s removal of self-perpetuating radicals. He restored the imprisoned Federalists rather than seizing power, and they held elections. Changing intervention served French control without erasing all domestic autonomy.

evidence.evidence_summary: Fructidor supplied the model for resolving political impasse: under French orchestration, troops surrounded the Convention and 22 Federalists were expelled on 22 January 1798.

subjects.label: Helvetic Republic: French intervention and imposed constitution
subjects.meaning: French conquest of northern Italy made Swiss Alpine communications strategically important. Ochs sought a unitary state partly to resist domination by France or Austria, while La Harpe promoted Vaud’s liberation from Berne; these aims were not identical with consent to a Swiss-wide settlement. French intervention against Berne and local resistance produced an imposed Helvetic constitution without national ratification or broad cantonal consent. French forces impounded city treasuries and gained lasting access to the passes, reversing the reformers’ hope of protection from external domination. Ochs and La Harpe sought limits on requisitions, and Ochs later supported a French militia demand that the legislature rejected; reformers’ influence did not ensure either restraint by France or domestic consent.
subjects.stance: French strategic needs and Swiss reformers' centralizing plans overrode older cantonal freedoms and local aims. Distinguish Ochs’s protective-centralization rationale, La Harpe’s Vaud campaign, local liberation aims and the eventual imposed state; Berne is a specific intervention, not a synonym for all Switzerland.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Alpine routes to occupied Italy transformed Swiss strategic value. Ochs proposed centralization as protection against great powers; La Harpe pursued Vaud’s release from Berne, while local revolts did not generally share a Swiss-wide unitary goal.

Brune was ordered to occupy Berne; French intervention suppressed resistance and imposed the Helvetic constitution without a ratifying convention. Cantonal refusal required further coercion, and access to Alpine passes entrenched French presence.

Ochs and La Harpe secured a promise against requisitions, yet city treasuries were impounded and war taxes imposed. Ochs later supported the French demand for 18000 militia auxiliaries, but the legislature authorized only volunteers, who fell far short. These outcomes contradicted hopes of protection from external domination.

subjects.label: Parthenopean Republic, 1799

subjects.label: End of the French Revolution through stability, peace, and reconciliation
subjects.meaning: The chapter's governing interpretation that the Revolution ended when Bonaparte supplied the stability, victorious peace, property security, political quiet, and religious reconciliation that the Directory could not. The chapter’s illustrative Seine-et-Oise report shows peasants attached to equality, release from seigneurial and hunting restrictions and acquired land, yet exhausted by war and civic participation. They wanted to retain these gains with peace and calm, not restore royal rule.
subjects.stance: The ending is presented as a political and social settlement completed by 1802, achieved at the substantial cost of representative and revolutionary principles, not as a single instantaneous event. The regional report illustrates this conditional attachment; it does not establish one uniform national peasant attitude.

The chapter closes with war ended, political strife eliminated, religious freedom restored, and contemporaries celebrating the Revolution's burial.

subjects.label: Military crisis, recovery, and disintegration of the Second Coalition
subjects.meaning: The defeats of 1799, Novi and Joubert’s death intensified political crisis; recovery in the Netherlands and Switzerland changed the balance. Austrian and Russian rivalry, failed joint strategy, and Paul I’s withdrawal then broke the coalition advantage and opened Bonaparte’s military and diplomatic opportunity. Renewed military success and confusion in the Councils gave Sieyès the more secure opening he sought for a coup to strengthen the executive.
subjects.stance: French recovery mattered, but allied division and selfish aims also explain the opening. Do not present victory as uninterrupted or attribute all coalition failure to Bonaparte.

evidence.evidence_summary: Joubert’s death and defeat at Novi, followed by coalition landings, deepened military and political emergency.

Victory over the Anglo-Russian invasion and divided Russian forces in Switzerland reversed the emergency; Sieyès saw the combination of military success and confused Councils as a ripe moment for constitutional change.
The improved military position creates the moment Sieyes believes suitable for an executive-strengthening coup.
Allied territorial interests and Austrian conduct obstructed coordinated exploitation of French weakness.
Russian withdrawal following disagreement and failed cooperation left Austria exposed to renewed French campaigning.
News of defeats pours into the Councils and intensifies the assault on the Directory.

subjects.label: Constitution of Year VIII and institutional design of the Consulate
subjects.meaning: The Year VIII constitution retained nominal suffrage through successive lists of eligible citizens while the Senate selected legislators. The Tribunate debated without voting, the Legislative Body voted without debate, and executive proposals came through the Council of State. The First Consul dominated the executive. Implementation preceded a manipulated plebiscite. The Senate embodied Sieyès’s intended conservative check on the legality of state action, yet its constitutional powers beyond selection were left obscure.
subjects.stance: Lists of eligibility did not let citizens choose their rulers. Divided legislative functions and lack of initiative preserved a representative appearance with little control; mass abstention and inflated returns preclude treating nominal ratification as genuine popular authorization.

evidence.evidence_summary: Successive eligibility lists replace direct electoral control; the Senate selects legislators and embodies Sieyès’s intended legality check, although its other powers are undefined. Separate chambers discuss and vote without legislative initiative.
The constitution operated before the plebiscite result; inflated approval and massive abstention supplied an appearance of assent rather than reliable consent.

subjects.label: Enlightenment origins and the project of national regeneration
subjects.meaning: An enlarged educated and critical reading public, with an expanding market for ideas, undermined confidence in a monarchy too little adapted to changing expectations. subjects.label: Nobility: loss of privilege and social transformation
subjects.meaning: The Revolution ended noble corporate status, feudal and fiscal privilege, venal ennoblement and automatic deference. Emigration, confiscation, execution and failed return caused trauma, but property recovery and later elite continuity limit any claim of total material destruction. Napoleon created a new nobility and incorporated surviving old nobles who could demonstrate landed wealth, an accommodation distinct from restoring their former corporate privileges or undoing emigrant losses. The Society of Thirty deliberately exploited divisions within the educated elite to mobilize support for an undivided legislature, helping convert a reform-minded order into a presumed enemy. Suspicion and imprisonment, followed in 1797 by civil-rights deprivation and threatened mass deportation on grounds of noble status, deepened the experience of persecution.
subjects.stance: Many nobles had supported reform before polemic cast aristocracy as a universal enemy. Nobles lost public monopoly and presumed social subordination more decisively than wealth; ending purchased ennoblement paradoxically made surviving social nobility more caste-like.

evidence.evidence_summary: The largely reform-minded nobility is cast as an enemy through anti-noble rhetoric and representation conflict; the Society of Thirty deliberately exploits elite tensions to mobilize support for an undivided legislature.

Nobles lost political, fiscal, feudal and heraldic privileges, and ending venal ennoblement made social nobility more caste-like. Many recovered property and remained large owners; Napoleon incorporated wealthy old nobles into his new nobility without restoring the former corporate order.

Exile, Quiberon, suspicion, imprisonment and executions deepened noble hostility. In 1797 nobles lost civil rights and nearly faced mass deportation merely for their status. Psychological displacement and loss of automatic deference proved more enduring than material losses.

subjects.label: Education: revolutionary disruption and decline
subjects.meaning: Revolutionary schemes for rational public education failed to replace the clerical institutions and revenues that were destroyed. The 1795 constitution abandoned the declared educational right of 1793; departmental central schools and higher schools only partly replaced destroyed institutions, while primary schooling depended on local initiative without public funding. subjects.label: Economic consequences of the French Revolution
subjects.meaning: Crisis, legislation, institutional destruction, inflation, and war made the Revolution an economic disaster that set French expansion back by a generation. The initial economic shocks also shaped hopes in the Estates-General, made cheap bread a test of Parisian patriotism, and turned rural fears into pressure for anti-feudal concessions.
subjects.stance: Some preconditions for later progress emerged, but the net short- and medium-term material effect for most people was destructive and precarious.

subjects.label: Landowners, bourgeoisie, and the property settlement
subjects.meaning: Landowners and especially bourgeois purchasers gained from abolition of dues, national-land sales, civil-law protection, and political systems grounded in property. Fear for the security of newly acquired property helped make a dictator’s guarantee of title and stability acceptable. These gains did not mean uniform bourgeois enrichment or complete noble impoverishment: many nobles remained major owners, and professional fortunes followed a separate, uneven course.
subjects.stance: The Revolution entrenched property as the chief social and political commodity while only modestly broadening small peasant ownership. The restored Bourbons accepted the alienated-land settlement, returning only unsold land and compensating losses.
acceptable_access: Bourgeois purchasers versus small peasant gains

evidence.evidence_summary: Abolished dues, codified property and ownership-based political rights benefited landowners. Bourgeois purchasers gained most from redistribution, and fear for their gains encouraged acceptance of dictatorial protection; noble wealth and the limited rise in small peasant ownership qualify any uniform class-transfer claim.
The restored Bourbons returned unsold émigré land and organized compensation, but did not seriously contemplate undoing the revolutionary land settlement.

subjects.label: Professions and the rise of bureaucracy
subjects.meaning: Abolition of venality compensated officeholders on underdeclared 1771 values, which also predated the subsequent rise in office prices, and largely in depreciating assignats, leaving them feeling cheated. The wider attack on corporations and validating institutions opened professions with minimal qualifications, enabling unqualified practice before Napoleonic licensing restored standards. War reversed early distrust of professional administration, greatly expanding a career bureaucracy with entry rules and pensions; bourgeois talent gained opportunities within a more bureaucratic state.
subjects.stance: Careers opened to bourgeois talent, but stable professional standards returned through a more bureaucratic Napoleonic state. The retrospective account also notes that stronger government and several rationalizing reforms were already developing or contemplated before 1789.

evidence.evidence_summary: Former venal officeholders received compensation based on underdeclared 1771 values, before the later rise in office prices, and largely in depreciating paper. Professional deregulation admitted unqualified practitioners until Napoleonic licensing; war also expanded administration and career rules.
The administrative career structure included rudimentary contributory pensions and offered a livelihood compared with the security of landed investment.
The counterfactual discussion notes that stronger government and several rationalizing reforms were already developing or contemplated before1789.

subjects.label: Protestant emancipation and religious equality
subjects.meaning: The Revolution established Protestant civil and religious equality despite dechristianization, regional conflict, and later Catholic reprisals. Protestant involvement in Federalism, revolutionary reprisals and Catholic restoration violence show that durable legal equality did not end this competition.
subjects.stance: The settlement was incomplete and disruptive, but pre-revolutionary Catholic legal dominance could not be restored. Consular salaried establishment also reduced Protestant democratic traditions and left isolated communities underserved.

required_access_facets.meaning: French power destroyed city-republics, secularized German states and transformed Dutch and Swiss institutions. Other changes were indirect: neighbors partitioned Poland while France appeared helpless, and the1798Irish rising precipitated loss of legislative independence. Imperial dissolution followed later Napoleonic victory.
required_access_facets.stance: Many territorial and constitutional changes outlasted French domination, but France surrendered most direct gains after 1815.
acceptable_access: Europe—territorial effects of the French Revolution

subjects.label: British ascendancy and the widening economic gap with France
subjects.meaning: Britain used sea power and war to appropriate markets and assets lost by France and its allies, consolidating nineteenth-century global predominance.
subjects.stance: British economic superiority was already emerging, but the Revolution widened the gap irrecoverably and made France's enemies major long-term beneficiaries.
acceptable_access: Great Britain—effects of the Revolutionary Wars

evidence.evidence_summary: Austria, Prussia, Britain, and other enemies retained gains while France lost most revolutionary conquests.
British naval and commercial power absorbed markets and resources, widening an existing lead over France.

subjects.label: Mass warfare, conscription, and expanded European states
subjects.meaning: Revolutionary mobilization turned war into an affair of nations and compelled rival governments to enlarge armies, taxation, policing, finance, and coercive capacity.
subjects.stance: National mobilization forced rival states to enlarge coercion, finance and recruitment. Clausewitz supplies a theory of removed limits; this is not a claim that every state instantly developed identical institutions.

evidence.evidence_summary: France mobilized national resources on a scale that forced other monarchies into mass warfare.
Conscription, militias, police, spies, taxation, and paper money expanded across states fighting France.
Arming the people and the emergencies of war revolutionized both the Revolution and the established European pattern of warfare.

subjects.label: Nationalism and national sovereignty
subjects.meaning: French expansion spread the doctrine of national sovereignty while provoking stronger counter-nationalisms, especially in Italy and among states resisting occupation.
subjects.stance: Revolutionary nationalism was both emancipatory and imperial; it taught subject peoples to mobilize against France in the same national terms. Existing Dutch patriotism and newly strengthened Italian national feeling followed different paths; Italian Jacobins were compromised by identification with the foreign power that initially encouraged their hopes.

evidence.evidence_summary: French occupation and nation-in-arms mobilization caused neighbours to answer with their own claims of sovereignty.
Italian nationalism and mass volunteering illustrate how nationalism resisted nationalism and produced future wars of peoples.

subjects.label: Popular sovereignty, democracy, and political legitimacy
subjects.meaning: The Revolution established the people as the ultimate source of sovereignty and made some display of popular consent increasingly necessary for political legitimacy. The author judges that the association of sansculotte direct action with coercion and bloodshed probably delayed wider acceptance of mass democracy among propertied observers, even while hereditary authority lost its unchallenged legitimacy.
subjects.stance: Democratic practice remained contested and often manipulated; sansculotte pressure frightened elites, yet hereditary prescription never fully recovered its old authority. This is a qualified claim about historical reception, not an assertion that democracy is inherently violent.

evidence.evidence_summary: The chapter presents popular sovereignty as the Revolution's globally victorious political message.

Memories of sansculotte coercion and bloodshed horrified propertied observers and probably retarded mass democracy’s acceptance; nevertheless rulers increasingly needed elections, plebiscites or other tokens of consent, often manipulated.

subjects.label: Liberty: ideals, symbols, and contradictions
subjects.meaning: Liberty encompassed freedom from arbitrary rule and freedoms of action, thought, writing, and worship, expressed through a durable revolutionary iconography.

subjects.label: Equality: abolition of privilege and property-based limits
subjects.meaning: Revolutionary equality abolished legal privilege and promoted equal rights and careers open to talent, but rejected economic equality and retained property-based political power.
subjects.stance: Its practical egalitarianism was transformative yet narrow, stopping well short of equality of fortune, broad democratic power, or equality between the sexes. Liberty and equality were early commitments; fraternity’s revolutionary prominence was later and brief.

subjects.label: Women: political participation and exclusion from equal rights
subjects.meaning: Women played decisive roles in journées, religious resistance, salons, clubs, and political writing but were excluded from equal political rights and confined ideologically to domestic roles. Nuns formed a cohesive center of resistance to the clerical oath, and lay women helped lead the late-1790s return to Catholic observance. Conflict between revolutionary clubwomen and market women accompanied the Convention’s ban on women’s organizations on 30 October 1793, a specific exclusion distinct from the Code’s later property restrictions.
subjects.stance: Women acted in popular journées, religious resistance, salons, clubs and rights advocacy, with divergent aims. Male authorities used ideas of female disorder and domestic duty to deny political equality; Bonaparte’s Code further restricted property rights. Do not equate every woman with every political camp or claim that de Gouges was executed simply for demanding women’s rights.

evidence.evidence_summary: The equality discussion identifies sex equality as largely dismissed despite women's unprecedented public role.

Women shaped journées, elite politics, clubs and rights advocacy; nuns resisted the oath and lay women led renewed observance. Conflict between revolutionary republican clubwomen and market women preceded the Convention’s 30 October 1793 ban on women’s organizations. Their roles and aims were diverse.
Contemporary prescriptions confined women to sex-specific domestic duties rather than political rights.

subjects.label: Birth of modern conservatism and counter-revolutionary ideology
subjects.meaning: The revolutionary assault on property, hierarchy, religion, and monarchy generated a self-conscious conservative theory and a transnational politics of order. De Maistre diagnosed abstract freedom and rationalism as sources of chaos and prescribed restoration of aristocracy, monarchy and above all Catholic religion, guarded vigilantly against renewed subversion.
subjects.stance: Intransigent restorationism often provoked the revolutions it sought to prevent, while moderate conservatives turned toward reform as prevention.

evidence.evidence_summary: Burke, Gentz and de Maistre developed explicit conservative arguments. De Maistre interpreted revolutionary history as a warning against abstract freedom and rationality and urged vigilant restoration of aristocracy, throne and altar.
Repressive intransigence spread across frontiers but drove blocked reformers toward renewed revolution; moderates favored reform instead.

subjects.label: The French Revolution as modern archetype and cultural tragedy
subjects.meaning: The Revolution became a model of deliberate political transformation and altered political culture, memory and imagined human agency. The author’s final assessment weighs courage and Enlightenment idealism against institutional destruction, mass death, and ruined lives in France and abroad. Its horrifying novelty included systematic governmental execution over months in a country celebrated for civilization and humane Enlightenment, distinct from the already familiar phenomenon of massacre.
subjects.stance: Preserve the double judgment: inspiring and ennobling yet appalling and tragic. Aggregate mortality and nonfatal suffering are central to the verdict. The closing figures are the author’s broad estimates, not an independent verified demographic calculation, and the argument does not reduce the Revolution to either triumph or failure.

evidence.evidence_summary: The chapter calls it the first modern and archetypal revolution whose influence made the post-1789 European world fundamentally different.

Distinctive ideology, popular democracy, mass war and Terror transformed political change. The source distinguishes familiar massacres from the shocking novelty of systematic government execution in a society renowned for humane civilization.

The conclusion estimates about a million French deaths by 1802, another million under Napoleon and further deaths abroad, alongside uncounted ruined lives. These costs qualify the founders’ courage and idealism within a deliberately tragic cultural assessment.

subjects.label: Toussaint L'Ouverture, restored slavery, and Haitian independence
subjects.meaning: Toussaint’s switch to the Republic and formerly enslaved troops drove out Spanish forces and established black military power, including violent punishment of collaborating whites and persecution of free people of colour. British intervention ended in withdrawal after devastating climate and disease losses, a separate failure. Toussaint was formally French-loyal but autonomous. Bonaparte’s reconquest captured him, yet disease, resistance renewed after news of slavery’s restoration, and renewed Anglo-French war defeated French control. Slavery was not re-established in Saint-Domingue; Haiti declared independence in 1804, followed by Dessalines’s imperial claim and another massacre of whites.
subjects.stance: Slavery was restored in other French colonies but never re-established in Saint-Domingue. Toussaint remained formally loyal to France while beyond its control; black military ascendancy did not ensure racial harmony. The author calls Haiti the only independent state directly created by the French Revolution, distinguishing later Latin American independence precipitated by Napoleon.
acceptable_access: Black military power--conflict with free coloureds
Slavery--restoration elsewhere and failure in Saint-Domingue

evidence.evidence_summary: Toussaint switched from Spain to the Republic after emancipation; black forces expelled the Spaniards and massacred whites who had welcomed them, establishing military power without ending racial violence.

British forces withdrew in 1798 after devastating disease and climate losses, with 13,000 dead; Toussaint’s formally loyal autonomy coexisted with persecution of free coloured people. French capture of Toussaint did not secure control: disease, news of 1802 slavery restoration and renewed war revived resistance. Haiti became independent with slavery unrestored; Dessalines later proclaimed himself emperor and ordered another massacre of whites.

subjects.label: Territorial mandates and post-paper deflation
subjects.meaning: After rejection of a land-bank proposal, territorial mandates exchanged at30assignats to one mandate but relied on unrealistic1790land values and excessive issue. Depreciated paper could buy land resold for cash, fuelling speculation. Mandates lost compulsory-tender status inJuly1796and were formally demonetized inFebruary1797; scarce coin then brought falling prices, high interest, debt pressure, barter and fiscal strain.
subjects.stance: A new name and land backing did not stabilize paper. Ending paper money replaced inflation with a different crisis rather than normal monetary conditions.

evidence.evidence_summary: Distrust of banking, including Lindet’s opposition, defeats a land-bank proposal. Mandates replace assignats at30:1with land priced at1790values, but excessive issue undermines the replacement.
Speculators convert depreciated paper into land and then cash. Compulsory tender ends inJuly1796and formal demonetization inFebruary1797, ending paper currency without restoring monetary normality.
Scarce coin as sole tender brought falling prices, high interest, crushing debts and barter; paper money’s disappearance created a different monetary crisis.

Post-paper specie scarcity undermines exchange and tax payment, forcing the government to seek cash through advances, asset sales and dependence on conquered territories; the debt settlement is a distinct fiscal response.
evidence.reconciliation_rationale: Reassign the page claim to its specific subject rather than the old composite endpoint. Specie scarcity and deflation belong to the post-paper phase.

required_access_facets.label: Territorial mandates and post-paper deflation
required_access_facets.meaning: After rejection of a land-bank proposal, territorial mandates exchanged at30assignats to one mandate but relied on unrealistic1790land values and excessive issue. Depreciated paper could buy land resold for cash, fuelling speculation. Mandates lost compulsory-tender status inJuly1796and were formally demonetized inFebruary1797; scarce coin then brought falling prices, high interest, debt pressure, barter and fiscal strain.

subjects.label: Preservation of colonial slavery in 1790
subjects.meaning: The Assembly preserved slavery on Barnave’s recommendation in 1790 despite its declaration of universal rights.
subjects.stance: This refusal of emancipation concerns enslaved people; it is distinct from the subsequent civil and political rights of free people of colour. Preservation of slavery must remain distinct from the separate legal question of political rights for free people of colour.

The Organic Articles imposed Gallican controls while the remaking of the episcopate strengthened papal authority. The negotiated Concordat and unilateral additions were distinct.

The settlement restored public Catholic worship and helped stabilize the regime, culminating symbolically in Easter 1802. It did not erase the lasting Catholic-republican polarization discussed on page 398.
The legislative purge removed opponents before the religious settlement was enacted and publicly celebrated, linking political coercion with the appearance of reconciliation.

The limited and then general rights conceded to free people of colour in 1791–1792 concerned already free people; wartime emancipation of enslaved people in 1793–1794 was a different subsequent transformation.

Haiti emerged directly from colonial revolution and resistance to restored slavery; Latin America drew revolutionary language and examples through a different process intensified by the later collapse of Spanish authority.
The collapse of paper purchasing power and fiscal effectiveness aggravated hunger and resentment under the Directory, alongside weather, blockade and military requisitions.

The collapse of paper revenue and deflation intensified tax failure and fiscal desperation before the bankruptcy. This is a setting for repudiation, not a claim that deflation alone dictated the policy.
Expanded resources support recovery without sufficing alone.

Preserving colonial slavery contradicted the universal-rights claim of 1789, whose principles were embodied in the completed 1791 settlement; the qualification concerns that rights legacy, not executive design.
relationships.target_facet: Principles of 1789 embodied in the completed constitutional settlement

relationships.rationale: Robespierre’s victory on free coloured political rights, not the earlier slavery decision, increases his standing.
Agricultural downturn and real-wage pressure deepen household insecurity; the relation concerns demand and livelihoods, not a claim that population caused individual crop failures.

Large commercial cultivators seek enclosure and concentrated use while villages defend collective grazing and other common rights; this is a conflict of uses, not a universal opposition between all farmers and all peasants.
Naval selection and technical competence contrast with the army officer corps’s purchase, social distance and uneven professional access; restrict the comparison to recruitment and competence.
Poor households’ expenditure on grain makes price rises dangerous and subsistence protest intelligible; precarious wages do not cause crop failure.
Legal, clandestine and foreign book supply circulates the works and criticism associated with Enlightenment; censorship persists and circulation does not equate to universal assent.

Defeat encourages inquiry into institutions and the postwar search for improvement; failed reform and subsequent conflicts deepen the later confidence crisis. Defeat is one contributor, not a sufficient cause.
The postwar inquest makes economic improvement a ministerial priority and helps give Physiocratic ideas an audience.
The longstanding Jansenist conflict supplies the Nouvelles ecclésiastiques example within the expanding press; it does not explain all journalism.
Religious prosecutions and attacks help cohere the philosophes’ sense of common cause despite doctrinal differences; changing orthodox piety remains a separate facet.
Prolonged intra-Catholic conflict and changes in piety accompany declining acceptance of persecution. The source does not establish a single sufficient cause of toleration.
Some philanthropic lodges, including the Nine Sisters, engage in campaigns against judicial injustice; this is not institutional support for every literary society.
The argument for intermediary bodies and checks on despotism informs interest in accountable provincial representation, without making Necker’s programme a direct transcription of Montesquieu.
Restored parlements fail to settle the confidence crisis, and representative provincial institutions become an alternative protection against administrative despotism.

State-led economic rationalization underlies enlightened administrative ambitions; arbitrary and unaccountable implementation creates opposition. This is contextual influence, not a claim that every intendant adopted the doctrine.

French reception of Franklin’s imagined simple life invoked Rousseauistic sylvan virtue. This is a specific idealization, not evidence that Rousseau supplied all American political language or caused the American Revolution.
Harvest fluctuation makes experiments in grain freedom politically vulnerable; distinguish shortage and subsistence unrest from the policy theory and conspiracy explanation.
Turgot warned against financing American intervention; Necker financed war through borrowing and cultivated public confidence. Compare fiscal strategies, not a personal quarrel.
Calonne’s coordinated tax, provincial and commercial programme addresses structural fiscal weakness; it was proposed and contested, not implemented by the Notables.
Necker’s published account of financial administration and reputation sharpen doubts about Calonne’s management; limit the claim to reputation and the accounting controversy.
The November 1787 Royal Session seeks registration of Brienne’s staged loan programme; a contested registration attempt is not successful implementation of the entire recovery plan.
Calls for the Estates-General increasingly make national consent the answer to taxation and credit problems, while the timing and political purpose of the demand change.

The failure to enforce the May judicial settlement disrupts justice and tax collection and helps close the treasury’s remaining credit channels; retain debt and harvest damage as additional pressures.
Clerical, noble, provincial and popular resistance presses for representation; the groups’ motives differ and cannot be reduced to one revolutionary ideology.
Treasury collapse leads to Necker’s recall because his public credit appears the only immediate remedy. It does not cause the Compte rendu published seven years earlier.
The July hailstorm undermines tax and credit expectations already weakened by debt, anticipations and political resistance.

Treasury centralization threatens established financiers, whose refusal of final advances contributes to collapse; this is a particular administrative mechanism, not a claim that every element of Brienne’s plan failed identically.
Sieyes gives the third estate’s claim to embody the nation an influential anti-privilege formulation; the pamphlet is an intervention in an existing mobilization.
Sieyes’s final appeal and roll call help turn verification deadlock into a claim of national representation; preserve the deputies’ collective action and broader constitutional setting.
Insistence on the 1614 order-based form turns a procedural and constitutional dispute into confrontation over privilege; it does not create the social orders.
The second Notables oppose doubling; the royal Result grants doubled third-estate representation while leaving voting procedure unresolved.
Pamphlets and petitions enlarge anti-privilege mobilization and national claims; print is a means of publicity rather than a sufficient cause of social conflict.
Doubling the third estate without deciding voting procedure leaves the verification dispute capable of becoming a struggle over separate orders and national authority.
Necker’s equivocation at the opening offers no authoritative decision on the central procedural issue, leaving deputies to contest verification.
Electoral assemblies prepare grievance lists alongside choosing deputies; electoral mobilization and cahier drafting are interlocking stages, not an abstract one-way cause of democratization.
Legal training equips leading third-estate deputies for the procedural dispute over verification and national legitimacy; it does not make their political outcome automatic.
Economic distress, high bread prices and shortages contribute to food disturbances during electoral mobilization; particular disturbances have local triggers.
Government procurement and contested trade rules form part of the supply context; do not flatten policy shifts and harvest shortage into a single cause of all bread politics.
Mirabeau’s journalism and defiant intervention support the Assembly’s resistance to royal commands; the refusal is collective and its success also depends on the king abandoning coercion.
Spectators and outside demonstrations sustain deputies resisting the Royal Session; this supplements the already authored crowd-to-Assembly formation relationship.
Failed dispersal and subsequent union of the orders defeat the royal constitutional strategy; effective coercive authority collapses later in July, not immediately in every sphere.
Troop concentration and Necker’s dismissal intensify fear of coercion and help prompt Paris electors’ militia preparations; the militia does not cause the earlier troop concentration.
Citizens organize militias in response to weak policing and disorder as well as court threat; the relation is not militia creation causing the prior breakdown of enforcement.
Scarcity and disorder contribute to provincial seizure and reconstitution of municipal power; Paris’s example, collapsing royal authority and local political motives also matter.
Direct action against seigneurial rights pressures the Assembly toward the night of renunciations; distinguish this pressure from the deputies’ legal qualifications and the continuing rural campaign.
Journalists and public agitation attack the Monarchiens’ constitutional proposals; the resulting suspensive veto is distinct from the full veto they advocated.
Tax and property qualifications restrict political participation and eligibility for elective offices; the franchise limits the reach of election, not the reverse.
The new direct-tax system’s weak enforcement and late collection aggravate the state’s financial crisis. Fiscal equality itself is not alleged to cause inherited debt.
Widespread evasion and resistance help make old indirect taxes and monopolies politically untenable, while reformers also act on egalitarian and economic principles.
Women act prominently in the October mobilization but remain excluded from the formal political franchise; retain this difference between popular intervention and legal citizenship.
State reorganization of the Church and the subsequent oath divide the earlier revolutionary coalition; distinguish the legal constitution from the later oath and regional reactions.
The oath operates as a public test of allegiance and reveals, as well as deepens, the breach in consensus; an opinion-poll metaphor is not a separate causal mechanism.
The failed flight and royal declaration expose repudiation of the Revolution and force another national choice; this compounds a religious and political breach already underway.
Dispossession and loss of independent clerical resources place the Church increasingly in state dependence and make salaried reorganization possible; they do not alone cause every later schism.

Pius privately warned of schism; later public letters stopped short of explicit condemnation but were received as decisive opposition and prompted withdrawals. Distinguish private warning, publication and reception.
Conflict over Avignon and the Comtat adds a territorial grievance to the ecclesiastical breach with Pius VI; the quarrels cannot be collapsed into a single doctrinal issue.
Publication of the papal break and oath withdrawals intensify suspicion of refractory worshippers; popular persecution is not simply execution of papal policy.
Harassment of refractory worship and conflict over religious liberty strengthen popular religious opposition to the Revolution; do not invert the old reinforced_by relation.

Catholic royalist mobilization around Montauban, Nîmes and Jalès supplies a southern instance of religious counter-revolution. It must not be subsumed geographically under the Vendée or western France.
Monastic inventories are a specific trigger in the Montauban conflict; the relationship is not an undifferentiated assertion that all Church-land sales caused the riot.
Religious equality alters the local political position of Protestants and intersects with Catholic reaction in the southern towns; equality as principle is distinct from the violent reaction.
The king’s religious and political alienation helps motivate escape; route planning, the Saint-Cloud confrontation and distrust are distinct contributing circumstances.
The flight activates the Jacobin network’s emergency vigilance and defense of the Revolution; subsequent club division is a different consequence.
Flight and repudiation sharpen republican demands and petition organization by Cordeliers and Social Circle activists; they did not organize the later massacre.
Republican petitioning challenges the Assembly’s preservation of monarchy and exposes divisions among former patriots; retain the precise dispute over restoration and national consent.
The Assembly’s kidnapping fiction and preservation of the crown allow moderates to complete a monarchical settlement; this is not the Constitution causing the earlier Varennes response.
Varennes heightens expectations and fears of foreign rescue that shape reception of later diplomacy. Pillnitz did not cause the earlier flight.
The king’s repudiation and continuing alienation make later constitutional acceptance suspect; the manifesto undermines confidence in the settlement, not vice versa.
The leaders’ move toward moderation and the fragmentation of earlier radical coalitions leave space for Robespierre’s distinct opposition and rise.
The August press restriction belongs to the restrictive aftermath of Champ de Mars; it does not cause the shooting or retrospectively authorize it.

The oath defined constitutional and refractory camps; elected staffing and career openings contrast with refusal and rival legitimacy. Regional shortages forced temporary reliance on refractories, and papal intervention prompted retractions.
The king’s confidence in Bouillé provides a military component of escape planning; army mutiny as a whole is not a cause of the king’s religious convictions.
Loss of officers makes the army’s weakness and foreign intervention more alarming; it does not cause the diplomatic Declaration itself.
Officer emigration worsens military leadership and cohesion later in 1791; it must not be projected backward as the cause of the earlier Nancy mutiny.

Lafayette collaborates with constitutional moderates in the final settlement; this does not erase conflict with radical crowds or transform his entire political career into support for one constitution.
The civic cult gives religious expression to republican virtue. This differs from the festival increasing suspicions of personal dictatorship.
Robespierre initially protected Danton and Desmoulins against excessive repression; this temporary alliance must not be conflated with his subsequent framing of their purge.
Evidence of Fabre’s fraud damaged the alignment between Robespierre and the Indulgents; real corruption must remain distinct from fabricated foreign conspiracy.
The defeat at Marseilles helped propel Toulon toward seeking British protection. This is an event sequence, not a claim that both cities shared a royalist programme.
Revolutionary armies requisitioned provisions and coerced suspected hoarders. The edge concerns enforcement of subsistence policy, not all wage or currency policy.
September popular pressure secured organization and activation of the Revolutionary Army previously accepted in principle; distinguish this from later subordination and dissolution.
Once immediate military crisis eased, Danton and Desmoulins urged moderation. This scoped late-1793 shift does not make every aspect of Terror a cause of indulgence.
Released suspects brought anti-Jacobin anger and support into the Gilded Youth milieu, without reducing the movement to one social origin.
Release and memories of Year II repression supplied revenge motives; the geographically varied White Terror was not wholly royalist or caused by release alone.

The forced loan withdrew purchasing power and contributed to temporary assignat recovery within the controlled economy. Do not attribute this realized effect to the unimplemented Ventôse confiscation scheme.
The republican calendar helped remove Christian temporal markers, while the wider dechristianizing campaign also included local coercion and later official retreat.
Virtue and preventive suspicion help explain the treatment of potential enemies in the Great Terror; this is not sole personal authorship or socially indiscriminate killing.
Babeuf used the unimplemented democratic constitution against Thermidorian retreat before the Directory conspiracy.
The destruction and exhaustion of militant organization before Germinal impaired the rising. Rebind from the post-Prairial repression unit, which occurs later and cannot cause Germinal’s failure.
Toulon workers mobilized against persecution but were defeated and executed. This responsive action differs from the same unit’s account of authorities enabling White Terror.
Factional conflict culminated in the coercive purge on 2 June; the Commission of Twelve was an earlier defensive step, not itself the final event.
Inflation, provision shortages and demands for controls sharpened sectional pressure on representation. Keep the 1793 political mobilization distinct from 1794 wage alienation.
Summer danger helped prompt the August levée en masse. Rebind the old compound levy endpoint to the August measure, excluding February conscription and later retrospective mass-war synthesis.
Chaumette linked municipal provisioning failure to the September mobilization; he did not command all popular actors.
Desmoulins and the Indulgents attacked Hébertist excess, amid reciprocal factional hostility; disagreement is not proof of the alleged foreign plots.
Robespierre supported governmental control and resisted religious coercion; rebind the old religious fragment to his political role rather than treating religion itself as an administrative actor.

The general’s betrayal sharpened the emergency that produced the Committee of Public Safety; this specifically preserves the institution’s creation rather than only the broader emergency-government consequence.
Paper depreciation deepened provisioning hardship alongside harvest, transport, winter and policy factors; it is not a sufficient explanation by itself.
The Supreme Being provided civic religion compatible with belief, in contrast with coercive dechristianization; official tolerance and local religious damage remained uneven.
Government consolidation addressed dispersed and self-sustaining coercion; centralization did not simply abolish Terror, and could intensify its use.
Destruction of popular rivals transferred control to government while Terror grew harsher; do not treat the Commune purge as termination of terror.
Final 1795 repression extinguished organized sansculotte force. Scope this edge to that final result, not the earlier erosion that helped defeat Hébert or Germinal.
Separation withdrew state payment for religion, including civic worship; this is a fiscal and institutional ending of official support, not an assertion that private belief vanished.
Thermidorian measures curtailed committee powers, judicial terror and local emergency organs; the coup-to-dismantling edge alone does not name the institutional object.
Chaumette’s eventual execution and the purge of the Commune followed his guarded response to insurrection; avoid labeling him an unqualified organizer of Hébert’s failed rising.
February conscription sparked western rural resistance with distinct Breton guerrilla development; it must not be rebound to August national mobilization.
Isolation, absences and fear of further denunciation helped produce the coalition against Robespierre; perceptions of dictatorship are not evidence of unlimited effective power.
The post-coup dismantling included repeal of 22 Prairial; the earlier law’s enactment and social effects are separate requirements.
The label federalist arose within disputes over legitimate national sovereignty; many rebels professed the same indivisible republic and did not seek federal government.
Saint-Just’s Ventôse proposals contemplated transfers from suspects to indigent patriots but were not carried out; this does not make him author of every emergency property measure.
Saint-Just presented the case against Hébertists within the government’s anti-faction campaign; retain allegations as allegations, not demonstrated foreign agency.
Exceptional interference with Danton’s defense foreshadowed the later law’s restriction of defendants’ protections; the earlier trial did not occur under that later law.
Blame for collective Terror was concentrated on selected former leaders, including prosecutions and deportation around Germinal; preserve the Convention’s own participation.
Pressure to restrain religious coercion was one motive for central government control; this specific religious connection is not exhausted by the broader Terror-centralization edge.
Restriction of popular institutions and radical leadership weakened independent sansculotte capacity before the final repression of Prairial 1795. Preserve the earlier erosion as a distinct process.

Defeat of Vendémiaire allowed the continuity arrangements to be carried through and former Convention members to retain legislative predominance. This consequence is distinct from the law helping provoke the rising.
Quelling domestic revolts absorbed forces in autumn 1793 and delayed the full effect of mass mobilization on the foreign fronts. This constraint differs from the emergency prompting recruitment.

relationships.rationale: Debt repudiation inflicted severe creditor losses; the accompanying fiscal reconstruction also alienated the property-owning constituency the Directory wished to secure.

relationships.rationale: Bonaparte restored slavery elsewhere and attempted to restore it in Saint-Domingue, reversing the emancipatory policy of 1794; black military resistance prevented the intended outcome in Saint-Domingue.
relationships.source_facet: Restoration of slavery and its failed imposition in Saint-Domingue

relationships.rationale: Campo Formio confirmed the disposal of Venice between French and Austrian interests, illustrating the limits of liberation promises.

The princes’ declarations and Louis XVIII’s restoration policy expressed an old-regime programme distinct from constitutional monarchism. Preserve the supplied pages’ differing dates without choosing an external correction.
relationships.target_facet: Restoration programme rather than constitutional alternative

relationships.rationale: The moralized treatment of potential enemies forms part of the context of the procedural severity of 22 Prairial; this is not sole personal authorship by Robespierre or an application of the law before enactment.
relationships.source_facet: Virtue and suspicion of potential enemies

synthesis.review_method: Full owned-page source-first reading,transparent reuse of previously inspected pages,complete review of both final-release entity lineages,then whole-book identity and dependency reconciliation. This is author synthesis,not independent approval.
synthesis.historical_release_choice: Neither release is selected as study winner. Native organizing units were a provisional scaffold; source-grounded changes and legacy refinements are explicitly dispositioned.

density_basis.metadata_correction: Semantic source-role note corrected without changing any verified count; frozen policy and independent source-scope disposition govern eligibility.

editorial_policy.unit: One coherent source argument,event,process,institution or developed group treatment. Merge repeated compatible phases only while preserving distinct source facets; split different legal populations,decisions,instruments or causal phases when one umbrella would obscure independent retrieval.
editorial_policy.access: Acceptable access terms are alternative routes to the specified facet,not interchangeable substitutes for every facet of a compound requirement. Required task facets retain their own exact subject scope. A broad umbrella without access to the asked distinction is insufficient.
editorial_policy.priority: Essential marks organizing explanations,central institutions or events and explicit major interpretive conclusions. Major marks substantial distinct developments and necessary subordinate mechanisms. Optional marks brief but useful distinct treatments. Incidental mentions remain scoped exclusions. No numerical priority quota or density target is used.
editorial_policy.relationships: Every new edge is explicitly authored with source pages and bounded meaning. Composite endpoints do not extend a relation beyond its stated facet. Retired historical edges may remain valid background or internal content without remaining separate graph requirements.
editorial_policy.tasks: Identical questions are consolidated with complete targets. Specific historical questions survive as explicit unweighted required-access facets where useful; generic interpretive templates are retired. A task attachment is not an assertion of question equivalence.
editorial_policy.source_ambiguity: Preserve uncertain motives,estimates,fluid labels and internal printed chronology conflicts. No outside factual correction silently replaces the supplied edition.
editorial_policy.density: The193118-word measurement supplies an operational prose-and-caption denominator only. Graph/map interiors, numbered keys and attribution-only credits are excluded from semantic evidence under frozen policy. Substantive literal captions and chapter text remain eligible independently of word-count convention; geography inferred only from excluded graphic regions is not required.

lineage_provenance.historical_discovery_claim: Existing histories preserved. These new artifacts record actual source re-examination and synthesis; they do not fabricate fresh historical discovery provenance.
lineage_provenance.candidate_unexposed_attestation: This author context and its two source authors inspected only the allowlisted source-only packet,methodology and authorized source-review/synthesis outputs. No candidate index,audit,score,result,name,ranking or outcome was inspected. Coordination concerning downstream workflow supplied no candidate content.
